title: Mexican Banks and Cryptocurrency Platforms Targeted With AllaKore RAT
content:
#### Description
A financially-motivated threat actor has been targeting Mexican banks and cryptocurrency trading entities with a modified version of AllaKore RAT. 

Lures use Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) naming schemas and links to legitimate, benign documents during the installation process. The AllaKore RAT payload is heavily modified to allow the threat actors to send stolen banking credentials and unique authentication information back to a command-and-control (C2) server for the purposes of financial fraud.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blogs.blackberry.com/en/2024/01/mexican-banks-and-cryptocurrency-platforms-targeted-with-allakore-rat

#### Publication Date
January 29, 2024

#### Author(s)
BlackBerry Research & Intelligence Team

enhanced.Incident: Mexican Banks and Cryptocurrency Platforms Targeted With AllaKore RAT
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause includes spear-phishing and drive-by download attacks that exploit user vulnerability in running malicious file attachments. The payload is a modified version of the open-source AllaKore RAT, customized for financial fraud. *The attackers use deceptive tactics, employing naming conventions from the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) and links to seemingly harmless documents* (https://redpiranha.net/news/threat-intelligence-report-january-30-february-5-2024). The malware is delivered via *a Microsoft software installer file* (https://cointelegraph.com/news/blackberry-mexican-crypto-exchanges-cyberthreat). *BlackBerry's Research and Intelligence Team flagged this threat, noting the malware sends stolen banking details to a command-and-control (C2) server* (https://cryptonews.com/news/blackberry-warns-mexican-bank-and-crypto-firms-on-potential-security-threat/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The threat actor is financially motivated and believed to be based in Latin America. The campaign utilizes Spanish-language instructions and infrastructure suggesting a local origin. *Numerous Mexico Starlink IPs are used, enhancing the campaign's local appearance* (https://redpiranha.net/news/threat-intelligence-report-january-30-february-5-2024).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The targeted organizations include banks, cryptocurrency trading platforms, and large companies in Mexico, particularly those with gross revenues over $100M USD. *Additionally, sectors such as retail, agriculture, public sector, manufacturing, transportation, commercial services, and capital goods are also targeted* (https://cointelegraph.com/news/blackberry-mexican-crypto-exchanges-cyberthreat). *The Mercian Social Security Institute (IMSS) is also directly involved due to the use of its links and naming conventions* (https://cryptonews.com/news/blackberry-warns-mexican-bank-and-crypto-firms-on-potential-security-threat/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The campaign has been ongoing since at least late 2021 and continues to be active.

MITRE TTPs.Defense Evasion: T1218.007 (Msiexec), T1480 (Execution Guardrails), T1070.004 (File Deletion), T1140 (Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information)
MITRE TTPs.Command and Control: T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer), T1071.001 (Web Protocols), T1219 (Remote Access Software)

enhanced.Impact: The specific number of records leaked or financial losses is not detailed, but the attack targets large financial entities, which could imply significant financial impact.

Mitigation.User awareness training: Educate employees about spear-phishing tactics and ensure they can recognize and avoid suspicious emails and links.
Mitigation.Email Filtering: Implement robust email filtering to detect and block malicious attachments and links.
Mitigation.Network Segmentation: Segment the network to limit the spread of malware.
Mitigation.Endpoint Protection: Deploy comprehensive endpoint protection solutions to detect and block malware execution.
Mitigation.Regular Updates: Ensure all systems and software are regularly updated to mitigate vulnerabilities.
Mitigation.Geolocation Verification: Implement geolocation checks for sensitive operations to detect and block anomalous access from unexpected regions.

Detection Signature.Incident: Mexican Banks and Cryptocurrency Platforms Targeted With AllaKore RAT

Internal checks.Setting1: Monitor for unexpected outbound connections to known C2 domains/IPs.
Internal checks.Setting2: Monitor for execution of suspicious MSI installers.
Internal checks.Setting3: Monitor for PowerShell execution with suspicious parameters.

title: MAR-10454006-r2.v1 SEASPY Backdoor
content:
#### Description
CISA obtained two SEASPY malware samples. The malware was used by threat actors exploiting CVE-2023-2868, a former zero-day vulnerability affecting versions 5.1.3.001-9.2.0.006 of Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG).

SEASPY is a persistent and passive backdoor that masquerades as a legitimate Barracuda service “BarracudaMailService” that allows the threat actors to execute arbitrary commands on the ESG appliance.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar23-209b

#### Publication Date
July 28, 2023

#### Author(s)
CISA

enhanced.Incident: SEASPY Backdoor
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause is the exploitation of CVE-2023-2868, a zero-day vulnerability affecting versions 5.1.3.001-9.2.0.006 of Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG). Attackers used this vulnerability to install SEASPY malware, a persistent and passive backdoor masquerading as a legitimate Barracuda service 'BarracudaMailService.' *The attackers can inject malicious reverse shell command via crafted TAR files* (https://teamt5.org/en/posts/cve-2023-2868-barracuda-email-security-gateway-vulnerability/). *Mandiant investigation revealed the attackers also used SALTWATER, SEASIDE, SUBMARINE, and WHIRLPOOL malware families in their campaign* (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/barracuda-esg-exploited-globally). *Additional malware families SKIPJACK and FOXTROT/FOXGLOVE were used for persistence and lateral movement* (https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2023-2868-barracuda-and-fbi-recommend-replacing-email-security-gateway-esg-devices). *Rapid7 incident response teams are investigating exploitation of Barracuda ESG appliances* (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/06/08/etr-cve-2023-2868-total-compromise-of-physical-barracuda-esg-appliances/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: *China-nexus UNC4841* (https://teamt5.org/en/posts/cve-2023-2868-barracuda-email-security-gateway-vulnerability/)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The affected organization is not explicitly mentioned, but it involves entities using Barracuda Email Security Gateway. *Targets include U.S. government entities, Chinese IT firms, research institutes in Taiwan, and Pakistani banks* (https://teamt5.org/en/posts/cve-2023-2868-barracuda-email-security-gateway-vulnerability/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The specific dates of the attack are not provided, but the report was released on July 28, 2023. *Attacks can be traced back to at least October 2022* (https://teamt5.org/en/posts/cve-2023-2868-barracuda-email-security-gateway-vulnerability/).
enhanced.Impact: The exact number of impacted devices or financial losses is not mentioned. *More than fifty thousand devices using Barracuda ESG are exposed to the vulnerability* (https://teamt5.org/en/posts/cve-2023-2868-barracuda-email-security-gateway-vulnerability/).
Mitigation: Maintain up-to-date antivirus signatures and engines.
Keep operating system patches up-to-date.
Disable File and Printer sharing services or use strong passwords/AD authentication if necessary.
Restrict users' ability to install and run unwanted software applications.
Enforce a strong password policy and implement regular password changes.
Exercise caution with email attachments, even if the sender appears known.
Enable a personal firewall on workstations, configured to deny unsolicited connection requests.
Disable unnecessary services on workstations and servers.
Scan for and remove suspicious email attachments; ensure the scanned attachment matches its true file type.
Monitor users' web browsing habits and restrict access to sites with unfavorable content.
Exercise caution when using removable media.
Scan all software downloaded from the Internet before executing.
Maintain situational awareness of the latest threats and implement appropriate Access Control Lists (ACLs).
*Barracuda recommends a full replacement of the impacted ESG regardless of the patch version* (https://teamt5.org/en/posts/cve-2023-2868-barracuda-email-security-gateway-vulnerability/).
*Barracuda began releasing containment and remediation patches on May 21, 2023* (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/barracuda-esg-exploited-globally).
*The FBI advises immediate replacement of compromised ESG appliances* (https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2023-2868-barracuda-and-fbi-recommend-replacing-email-security-gateway-esg-devices).
*Rotate any credentials connected to the ESG appliance* (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/06/08/etr-cve-2023-2868-total-compromise-of-physical-barracuda-esg-appliances/).

Internal checks: Verify the legitimacy of the 'BarracudaMailService' on all Barracuda ESG appliances.
Monitor for unusual or unauthorized network traffic on ports 25 and 587.
Check for the presence of the SEASPY malware using provided YARA rules and hash values.
External scanning: Scan for anomalies in network traffic patterns, especially connections to unknown or suspicious IP addresses.
Look for the reverse shell traffic initiated by the malware.
Detection Signature.*107.148.219.227* (https://teamt5.org/en: YARA Rules: rule CISA_10452108_01 : SEASPY backdoor communicates_with_c2 installs_other_components {'}}

title: Active Exploitation of Cisco IOS XE Software Web Management User Interface Vulnerability
content:
#### Description
Cisco has identified active exploitation of a previously unknown vulnerability in the Web User Interface (Web UI) feature of Cisco IOS XE software (CVE-2023-20198) when exposed to the internet or untrusted networks. This affects both physical and virtual devices running Cisco IOS XE software that also have the HTTP or HTTPS Server feature enabled. Successful exploitation of this vulnerability allows an attacker to create an account on the affected device with privilege level 15 access, effectively granting them full control of the compromised device and allowing possible subsequent unauthorized activity.  

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/active-exploitation-of-cisco-ios-xe-software/


#### Publication Date
October 16, 2023

#### Author(s)
Cisco Talos

enhanced.Incident: Active exploitation of Cisco IOS XE Software Web Management User Interface vulnerabilities
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause includes vulnerabilities in the Web User Interface (Web UI) feature of Cisco IOS XE software, specifically CVE-2023-20198 (CVSS Score: 10.0) and CVE-2023-20273 (CVSS Score: 7.2). These vulnerabilities allow privilege escalation and command injection due to the HTTP or HTTPS Server feature being enabled on internet or untrusted network-facing devices (Cisco Bug ID: CSCwh87343) *The changes* (https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-iosxe-webui-privesc-j22SaA4z).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Information about the specific threat actor is not provided. The campaign involves the use of a Lua-based web shell named 'BadCandy.'
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Cisco devices running IOS XE software were targeted. The specific organizations affected are not disclosed.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The activity was observed early as September 18, 2023, with cases identified until November 2, 2023.
enhanced.Impact: The exact number of devices or the financial losses are not detailed, but the impact includes unauthorized access, implant deployment, and potential loss of control over affected devices. *PoC for CVE-2023-20273 released* (https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2023-20198-zero-day-vulnerability-in-cisco-ios-xe-exploited-in-the-wild).
Mitigation: Disable the HTTP/HTTPS server feature on internet-facing systems.
Apply patches for CVE-2023-20198 and CVE-2023-20273 as provided by Cisco's Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT).
Regularly monitor and audit device configurations for unauthorized user accounts.
Implement network segmentation to reduce exposure of management interfaces to untrusted networks.
Use Snort rules provided by Cisco for detection and prevention. *Horizon3.ai PoC release* (https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2023-20198-zero-day-vulnerability-in-cisco-ios-xe-exploited-in-the-wild).
Detailed Steps for Mitigation: Disable HTTP/HTTPS server feature:
```shell
no ip http server
no ip http secure-server
Apply firmware updates as per Cisco’s PSIRT advisory.
Regularly check for unauthorized users:
```shell
show running-config | include username

Implement network segmentation and use firewalls to limit access to management interfaces. *First Fixed Version 17.9.4a* (https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2023-20198-zero-day-vulnerability-in-cisco-ios-xe-exploited-in-the-wild).

Setting3: Check for installed implants or unusual configuration files.
External scanning:
Detect open HTTP/HTTPS ports on devices.
Use Snort rules to identify exploitation attempts and interactions with implants.

title: Fake CVE-2023-40477 Proof of Concept Leads to VenomRAT
content:
#### Description
Researchers should be aware of threat actors repurposing older proof of concept (PoC) code to quickly craft a fake PoC for a newly released vulnerability. On Aug. 17, 2023, the Zero Day Initiative publicly reported a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in WinRAR tracked as CVE-2023-40477. They had disclosed it to the vendor on June 8, 2023. Four days after the public reporting of CVE-2023-40477, an actor using an alias of whalersplonk committed a fake PoC script to their GitHub repository.

The fake PoC meant to exploit this WinRAR vulnerability was based on a publicly available PoC script that exploited a SQL injection vulnerability in an application called GeoServer, which is tracked as CVE-2023-25157. Palo Alto analyzed the fake PoC script and all the links in the infection chain, which ultimately installed a VenomRAT payload.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/fake-cve-2023-40477-poc-hides-venomrat/

#### Publication Date
September 19, 2023

#### Author(s)
Robert Falcone

enhanced.Incident: Fake CVE-2023-40477 PoC Leads to VenomRAT
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause is a fake proof of concept (PoC) script for CVE-2023-40477, containing a malicious payload. The PoC, disguised to exploit a WinRAR vulnerability, executed a script delivering VenomRAT malware. It was based on an existing PoC for CVE-2023-25157, with added malicious code. Hosted files on `checkblacklistwords[.]eu` and created a *scheduled task named Windows.Gaming.Preview* (https://hackread.com/fake-poc-script-researchers-download-venomrat/). *VenomRAT can steal cryptocurrency wallets, browser cookies, credit card details, and data from FileZilla FTP* (https://www.cybersecurity-help.cz/blog/3511.html).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: An unknown threat actor using the alias 'whalersplonk'.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Cybersecurity researchers and potentially other opportunistic actors.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The fake PoC was committed to GitHub on August 21, 2023, four days after the CVE-2023-40477 vulnerability was publicly announced. *The actor uploaded a video to Streamable demonstrating use of the fake PoC script* (https://hackread.com/fake-poc-script-researchers-download-venomrat/).
MITRE TTPs: T1059.001 - Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1059.007 - Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript/JScript
T1071.001 - Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
enhanced.Impact: The impact is difficult to quantify, but the instructional video provided by the actor had 121 views, indicating potential compromises.
Mitigation: Always verify the authenticity of PoC scripts before running them.
Use trusted sources for downloading PoCs.
Implement endpoint protection solutions that can detect and block malicious scripts and RATs.
Regularly update software and apply patches to mitigate known vulnerabilities.
Educate users and researchers about the risks of running unverified scripts from the Internet.

Detection Signature.Incident: Fake CVE-2023-40477 PoC Leads to VenomRAT
Detection Signature.Signature name: Fake CVE-2023-40477 PoC with VenomRAT Payload
Internal checks: Verify the integrity and authenticity of downloaded PoC scripts.
Monitor for unusual script executions and network connections to suspicious domains.
External scanning: Monitor for domains such as `checkblacklistwords[.]eu` hosting malicious files.
Check for communications with known C2 IPs like `94.156.253[.]109`.

Additional Information: Security researchers at Palo Alto Networks discovered the new malware campaign targeting CVE-2023-40477 vulnerability in WinRAR (https://hackread.com/fake-poc-script-researchers-download-venomrat/).

The fake PoC script was first discovered by @AabyssZG, a Chinese cybersecurity researcher and founder of Yuanlong Sec Security Team (AabyssTeam) (https://hackread.com/fake-poc-script-researchers-download-venomrat/).

title: LokiBot Campaign Targets Microsoft Office Document Using Vulnerabilities and Macros
content:
#### Description
In a recent investigation, FortiGuard came across several malicious Microsoft Office documents designed to exploit known vulnerabilities. Specifically, CVE-2021-40444 and CVE-2022-30190 are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Exploiting these vulnerabilities allowed the attackers to embed malicious macros within Microsoft documents that, when executed, dropped the LokiBot malware onto the victim's system.

LokiBot, also known as Loki PWS, has been a well-known information-stealing Trojan active since 2015. It primarily targets Windows systems and aims to gather sensitive information from infected machines.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/lokibot-targets-microsoft-office-document-using-vulnerabilities-and-macros

#### Publication Date
July 17, 2023

#### Author(s)
Cara Lin

enhanced.Incident: LokiBot Campaign Targets Microsoft Office Document Using Vulnerabilities and Macros
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident includes the exploitation of known remote code execution vulnerabilities in Microsoft Office documents, specifically CVE-2021-40444 and CVE-2022-30190 (Follina). These vulnerabilities allowed attackers to embed malicious macros within Microsoft documents, which, when executed, dropped the LokiBot malware onto the victim's system. *FortiGuard Labs* (https://hackread.com/lokibot-malware-malicious-macros-word-docs/) discovered the campaign and revealed the use of *Cuttly URL shortener* (https://hackread.com/lokibot-malware-malicious-macros-word-docs/) to redirect to *GoFile cloud file-sharing* (https://hackread.com/lokibot-malware-malicious-macros-word-docs/). *Ankura Consulting Group, LLC* (https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=ee99f093-c472-431d-9c20-04dc6898bd14) noted that one document contained an *embedded link within an XML file* while another used a *VBA script to download an injector*.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Likely cybercriminals using LokiBot malware. Specific threat actor/group not mentioned.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: *Healthcare sector* (https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/lokibot-malware-analyst-note-tlpclear.pdf); Windows users globally.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The campaign was identified in May 2023.
enhanced.MITRE TTPs:
- T1203 (Exploitation for Client Execution)
- T1059.005 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic)
- T1071 (Application Layer Protocol)
- T1027 (Obfuscated Files or Information)
- T1055 (Process Injection)
- T1070 (Indicator Removal on Host)
enhanced.Impact: Control and collection of sensitive information from a victim’s device, including *data exfiltration* (https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/lokibot-malware-analyst-note-tlpclear.pdf). The exact number of impacted devices or financial losses is not mentioned.
enhanced.Mitigation:
- Keep Microsoft Office applications and Windows operating systems updated with the latest security patches.
- Disable macros in Microsoft Office documents by default and only enable them if absolutely necessary and from trusted sources.
- Use advanced endpoint protection solutions like FortiGuard to detect and block malware.
- Educate users on the risks of opening documents from unknown sources and clicking on suspicious links.
- Implement network security measures to block access to known malicious C2 servers and IP addresses.
enhanced.Detection Signature:
- Service: Microsoft Office
- Severity: Critical
- Incident: LokiBot Campaign
- Signature name: “Malicious Macro in Microsoft Office Document”
- Internal checks:
    - Setting1: Ensure macros are disabled by default in Microsoft Office applications.
    - Setting2: Regularly scan for known vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-40444, CVE-2022-30190) and apply patches.
    - Setting3: Monitor for unusual Office document behavior such as new processes being spawned.
- External scanning:
    - Scan for vulnerable versions of Microsoft Office.
    - Monitor for communication with known malicious C2 servers.
enhanced.Additional Information: *TLP:WHITE* (https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/lokibot-malware-analyst-note-tlpclear.pdf). *Lure images of Word error* (https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=ee99f093-c472-431d-9c20-04dc6898bd14) were used to trick users into enabling editing.

title: Malicious Batch File (.bat) Disguised as a Document Viewer Being Distributed (Kimsuky) - ASEC BLOG
content:
#### Description
AhnLab Security Emergency response Center (ASEC) has confirmed the distribution of malware in the form of a batch file (*.bat). This malware is designed to download various scripts based on the anti-malware process, including AhnLab products, installed in the user’s environment. Based on the function names used by the malware and the downloaded URL parameters, it is suspected to have been distributed by the Kimsuky group.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/55219/


#### Publication Date
July 10, 2023

#### Author(s)
ye_eun

enhanced.Incident: Malicious Batch File (*.bat) Disguised as a Document Viewer Being Distributed (Kimsuky)
enhanced.Root cause: The incident was caused by a phishing campaign distributing malicious batch files disguised as document viewers like docview.bat, pdfview.bat, and hwp.bat. The batch files were designed to download various scripts based on the anti-malware process installed in the user's environment using the *WMIC command* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/jp/55207/). The campaign also involved *APT37* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/ATIP_2023_Jul_Threat-Trend-Report-on-Kimsuky-Group.pdf) and utilized *LNK file tactics* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/ATIP_2023_Jul_Threat-Trend-Report-on-Kimsuky-Group.pdf).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Kimsuky
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Not specified, but targets included individuals handling *military, unification documents* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/jp/55207/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Identified between Mar. 22, 2023, and Jun. 21, 2023
enhanced.Impact: The exact number of records or financial losses is not specified, but the impact includes potential unauthorized access to sensitive military and unification-related documents.
Mitigation: Implement email filtering to block phishing emails and malicious attachments.
Regularly update anti-malware software to detect and block malicious scripts.
Educate users on recognizing and avoiding phishing attempts.
Use multi-factor authentication to reduce the risk of unauthorized access.
Monitor network traffic for access to suspicious URLs and block them.
Regularly audit and update security policies to include the latest threat intelligence.

Detection Signature.Service: Not applicable to a specific service (Phishing and Malware detection)
Detection Signature.Incident: Distribution of malicious batch files disguised as document viewers
Internal checks: Monitor for execution of batch files from email attachments.
Check for unusual network connections to external URLs, especially Google Drive and suspicious domains.
Inspect for modifications to startup scripts and registry entries related to persistence.
External scanning: Monitor and block access to known malicious URLs (e.g., joongang.site, namsouth.com, staradvertiser.store)
Detect suspicious downloads from Google Drive and Docs. *C2 servers* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/ATIP_2023_Jul_Threat-Trend-Report-on-Kimsuky-Group.pdf).

title: Trojanized Free Download Manager Found to Contain a Linux Backdoor
content:
#### Description
Kaspersky researchers analyzed a Linux backdoor disguised as Free Download Manager software that remained under the radar for at least three years.  Kaspersky discovered the subdomain ' deb.fdmpkg[.]org' that claims to host a Debian repository of a piece of software called ‘Free Download Manager’.  This script drops two ELF files and then establishes persistence by creating a cron task that launches an executable every 10 minutes.  This executable is a backdoor, and it does not import any functions from external libraries. Using this backdoor, Kaspersky determined that the attackers then deployed a Bash stealer.  This stealer collects data such as system information, browsing history, saved passwords, cryptocurrency wallet files, as well as credentials for cloud services (AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Azure).

Kaspersky checked the official website of Free Download Manager (freedownloadmanager[.]org). Packages available for download from this website turned out to be hosted on the files2.freedownloadmanager[.]org domain, and were not backdoored.  Kaspersky found several social media posts of users who were redirected from the legitimate site download page to the malicious URL that hosts the infected version of Free Download Manager.  Kaspersky noted that the redirection to the malicious domain was not occurring in all cases. Thus, it is possible that the malware developers scripted the malicious redirection to appear with some degree of probability or based on digital fingerprint of the potential victim.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://securelist.com/backdoored-free-download-manager-linux-malware/110465/

#### Publication Date
September 12, 2023

#### Author(s)
Leonid Bezvershenko  
Georgy Kucherin

enhanced.Incident: Free Download Manager Backdoored – A Possible Supply Chain Attack on Linux Machines
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident was a malicious Debian repository. An infected Debian package for Free Download Manager was distributed via a subdomain (deb.fdmpkg[.]org). The package contained malicious scripts that installed a backdoor and a stealer on the victim's system. *The cybersecurity firm Kaspersky Lab identified the compromise* (https://www.freedownloadmanager.org/blog/?p=664). *The malware established a reverse shell to a C2 server and the crond backdoor launched the /var/tmp/bs executable for SSL/TCP communications* (https://hackread.com/free-download-site-pushed-linux-password-stealer/). *Kaspersky experts discovered the attackers used YouTube installation guides to spread the malware* (https://securitybrief.com.au/story/kaspersky-uncovers-3-year-old-supply-chain-attack-campaign). *Comments in Russian and Ukrainian, including information about improvements made to the malware, were found in the postinst script* (https://securityaffairs.com/150851/malware/free-download-manager-supply-chain-attack.html).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Not explicitly named in the report. The backdoor is a modified version of the Bew backdoor, known since 2013. *A Ukrainian hacker group exploited a script vulnerability* (https://www.freedownloadmanager.org/blog/?p=664). *The attackers utilized digital fingerprints to selectively infect users* (https://securitybrief.com.au/story/kaspersky-uncovers-3-year-old-supply-chain-attack-campaign). *The Bash stealer was analyzed by Yoroi in 2019* (https://hackread.com/free-download-site-pushed-linux-password-stealer/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Linux users globally, including in Brazil, China, Saudi Arabia, and Russia.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The malicious package was distributed from at least January 2020 to 2022. *The vulnerability was unknowingly resolved during a site update in 2022* (https://www.freedownloadmanager.org/blog/?p=664).
MITRE TTPs: T1059.004 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell)
enhanced.Impact: The exact number of devices impacted is unclear; the campaign has victims in multiple countries. *Less than 0.1% of users were affected* (https://www.freedownloadmanager.org/blog/?p=664). *The malware collected various types of data, including system information, browsing history, saved passwords, cryptocurrency wallet data, and cloud services credentials* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/free-download-manager-site-redirected-linux-users-to-malware-for-years/).
Mitigation: Ensure that software is downloaded from verified and trusted sources.
Regularly audit and monitor systems for unusual cron jobs or other signs of modifications.
Implement security solutions that can detect and prevent malware on Linux systems.
Verify the integrity of downloaded packages using checksums.
Regularly update and patch systems to avoid exploitation of known vulnerabilities. *Utilize the provided bash script for malware check* (https://www.freedownloadmanager.org/blog/?p=664).

*Refer to the FDM team statement for further guidance* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/free-download-manager-site-redirected-linux-users-to-malware-for-years/). *Security expert Georgy Kucherin emphasizes the need for robust Linux protection measures* (https://securitybrief.com.au/story/kaspersky-uncovers-3-year-old-supply-chain-attack-campaign). *The Free Download Manager team apologized to users and urged them to scan their systems and update passwords* (https://hackread.com/free-download-site-pushed-linux-password-stealer/).

Internal checks: Monitor DNS queries to suspicious domains like fdmpkg[.]org.
Check for unusual cron jobs (e.g., /etc/cron.d/collect).
Verify the integrity of binaries in /var/tmp (e.g., crond, bs).
External scanning: DNS queries to fdmpkg[.]org.
Check for connections to secondary C2 server (e.g., 172.111.48[.]101).

title: Arid Viper  APT’s Nest of SpyC23 Malware Continues to Target Android Devices
content:
#### Description
The Arid Viper group has a long history of using mobile malware, including at least four Android spyware families and one short-lived iOS implant, Phenakite. The SpyC23 Android malware family has existed since at least 2019, though shared code between the Arid Viper spyware families dates back to 2017. It was first reported in 2020 by ESET in a campaign where the actor used a third-party app store to distribute weaponized Android packages (APK). That campaign featured several apps designed to mimic Telegram and Android application update managers.

Through 2022 and early 2023, Arid Viper developed several newer SpyC23 versions that share these themes: two apps mimick Telegram, while another is internally called APP-UPGRADE but is based on a romance-themed messaging app called Skipped Messenger. Cisco Talos recently reported on the history of Skipped Messenger, revealing that the once-benign dating application was likely passed from the original developer to the Arid Viper actor.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/arid-viper-apts-nest-of-spyc23-malware-continues-to-target-android-devices/

#### Publication Date
November 6, 2023

#### Author(s)
Alex Delamotte

Incident: Arid Viper | APT\u2019s Nest o.Root cause: The root cause involves distributing malware through weaponized Android apps posing as legitimate applications like Telegram, Threema, or dating apps such as Skipped Messenger. These apps request excessive permissions, giving the malware high control over the victim's device. The malware is also spread via a fake Android app store named DigitalApps. *Arid Viper disguises malware as updates for non-malicious apps, leveraging Google’s Firebase messaging system for C2 operations. They also employ anti-decompilation and anti-virtualization techniques* (https://redskyalliance.org/xindustry/arid-viper) *and dismiss notifications from built-in Android security apps* (https://techxmedia.com/eset-research-reveals-new-android-spyware-masked-as-threema-and-telegram/).
Incident: Arid Viper | APT\u2019s Nest o.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Arid Viper, an espionage-motivated threat actor with Hamas-aligned interests, also known as APT-C-23 or Two-tailed Scorpion, is believed to be based out of Gaza. *They use ALFA TEaM Shell for administering malicious domains and have a history of using multiple Android spyware families including GnatSpy, FrozenCell, and VAMP* (https://redskyalliance.org/xindustry/arid-viper).
Incident: Arid Viper | APT\u2019s Nest o.Organization/industry/location: The primary targets are individuals in the Middle East, including military personnel, journalists, and dissidents, particularly Arabic speakers.
Incident: Arid Viper | APT\u2019s Nest o.Start date \u2013 End date: The campaign has been ongoing through 2022 and 2023, with earlier versions of the malware dating back to 2017. *The malware shares infrastructure with Skipped GmbH’s apps and includes a non-weaponized version of Skipped Messenger* (https://redskyalliance.org/xindustry/arid-viper) *and was also being analyzed by ESET researchers since April 2020* (https://techxmedia.com/eset-research-reveals-new-android-spyware-masked-as-threema-and-telegram/).
MITRE TTPs: TTPs associated with social engineering and spear-phishing (T1204)
Exploitation of mobile devices through malicious applications (T1476)
Collection of device information and surveillance (T1512)
Command and Control via legitimate services (T1071)
Incident: Arid Viper | APT\u2019s Nest o.Impact: The impact is not quantified in terms of financial losses or the number of devices affected, but the malware provides significant spying capabilities, compromising personal and sensitive information of the victims. *It disables security notifications on Samsung devices* (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/arid-viper-mobile-spyware/).
Mitigation: Avoid installing applications from third-party sources or outside of the Google Play Store.
Carefully review permissions requested by applications and only grant necessary permissions.
Use reputable mobile security solutions to detect and prevent spyware.
Keep the device's operating system and applications updated to the latest versions.
Enable Google Play Protect on Android devices.
Educate potential targets about the risks of malware and the importance of cybersecurity hygiene.

Detection Signature.Signature name: Malicious Android Application with Excessive Permissions
Internal checks: Monitor for applications requesting excessive permissions such as access to contacts, microphone, location, and storage.
Regularly audit installed applications for any suspicious behavior or permissions.
Implement mobile threat defense solutions that can detect and block malicious apps. *Look for apps mimicking the Juola/Skipped App* (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/arid-viper-mobile-spyware/).

External scanning.No specific port scanning applicable for: Monitor download sources for known malicious APKs and hash values.

title: New Wave of SocGholish Infections Impersonates WordPress Plugins
content:
#### Description
A new wave of SocGholish malware infections has been identified, targeting WordPress websites. The malware campaign leverages a JavaScript malware framework that has been in use since at least 2017. The malware attempts to trick unsuspecting users into downloading what is actually a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) onto their computers, which is often the first stage in a ransomware infection. The infected sites were compromised through hacked wp-admin administrator accounts.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.sucuri.net/2024/03/new-wave-of-socgholish-infections-impersonates-wordpress-plugins.html

#### Publication Date
March 1, 2024

#### Author(s)
Ben Martin

enhanced.Incident: New Wave of SocGholish Infections Impersonates WordPress Plugins
enhanced.Root cause: Compromised wp-admin credentials and installation of malicious plugins impersonating legitimate WordPress plugins.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: SocGholish malware campaign, *Evil Corp* (https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/socgholish/)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: WordPress websites (specific organization/industry/location not mentioned)
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: October 2023 – March 2024, *peak in March 2023* (https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/socgholish/)
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1059.007: Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript
enhanced.Impact: Over 2,800 detections in the current year, significant increase from 1,400 detections in the previous year.
Mitigation: Secure your wp-admin panel by using strong and unique passwords.
Regularly update your WordPress core, plugins, and themes to the latest versions.
Enable automatic updates for plugins and themes whenever possible.
Employ a regular backup system to ensure data recovery in case of an incident.
Implement a website firewall to block malicious traffic and patch known vulnerabilities.
Avoid downloading and installing plugins and themes from unofficial sources.
Monitor access logs for unusual login attempts and plugin installations.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: Change all wp-admin passwords to strong, unique passwords.
Update the WordPress core, plugins, and themes to the latest versions.
Enable automatic updates in the WordPress admin dashboard.
Set up a regular backup schedule and ensure backups are stored securely.
Install and configure a reputable website firewall.
Remove any plugins or themes not obtained from official sources.
Regularly review access logs for any suspicious activity.
Educate users on the importance of downloading updates only from official sources.

Internal checks: Monitor for unauthorized login attempts to wp-admin.
Alert on the installation of plugins from non-official sources.
Monitor wp_postmeta table for suspicious script tags.
External scanning: Scan for malicious JavaScript loaded from known SocGholish domains.
Monitor network traffic for connections to known malicious domains.

New information: *Fake update alerts, Cobalt Strike framework, code injection in werfault.exe* (https://secure.wphackedhelp.com/blog/fakeupdates-socgholish-malware/)

title: Malware Spotlight Linodas aka DinodasRAT for Linux
content:
#### Description
Check Point Research has analyzed the latest Linux version (v11) of DinodasRAT, which is a cross-platform backdoor that was observed in attacks by the Chinese threat actor LuoYu.

The malware is more mature than the Windows version, with a set of capabilities tailored specifically for Linux servers. The latest version introduces a separate evasion module to hide any traces of malware in the system by proxying and modifying the system binaries’ execution. The malware is installed on Linux servers as a way for the threat actors to gain an additional foothold in the network. 

DinodasRAT was initially based on the open-source project called SimpleRemoter, a remote access tool based on the Gh0st RAT, but with several additional upgrades. 

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://research.checkpoint.com/2024/29676/

#### Publication Date
March 31, 2024

#### Author(s)
Check Point Research

enhanced.Incident: Malware Spotlight: Linodas aka DinodasRAT for Linux
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident includes the use of a cross-platform backdoor named DinodasRAT (Linux variant known as Linodas) installed on Linux servers. The malware achieves persistence through various methods, including modifying system files and configurations to maintain a foothold and avoid detection. *The malware also employs the Tiny Encryption Algorithm (TEA) for encrypting C2 communications* (https://www.enigmasoftware.com/dinodasrat-removal/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The attack was carried out by a Chinese-nexus cyber espionage threat actor focusing on Southeast Asia, Africa, and South America. This group shows significant alignment with the threat actor 'Earth Krahang' and has been linked to the Chinese threat actor 'LuoYu.' *Additionally, they have been involved in Operation Jacana, targeting a governmental body in Guyana* (https://www.enigmasoftware.com/dinodasrat-removal/). *The group UNC3886 has also exploited CVE-2023-34048 since late 2021* (https://vx-underground.org/APTs/2024).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The specific organizations or industries targeted are not explicitly mentioned, but the focus is on regions such as Southeast Asia, Africa, and South America. *This includes targeting Red Hat-based distributions and Ubuntu Linux* (https://www.enigmasoftware.com/dinodasrat-removal/). *Additionally, the Earth Preta Campaign targets Asia* (https://vx-underground.org/APTs/2024).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The earliest Linux version was first seen in the wild in July 2021, with subsequent versions identified up to November 2023.
MITRE TTPs: T1547: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
enhanced.Impact: The specific number of devices or financial losses is not mentioned, but the malware is used for cyber espionage, potentially impacting numerous organizations and systems within the targeted regions. *DinodasRAT has evolved from an open-source project known as SimpleRemoter, rooted in Gh0st RAT* (https://www.enigmasoftware.com/dinodasrat-removal/).

Secure Configuration: Regularly audit and secure system configurations to prevent unauthorized changes.
Ensure that only necessary services are active and properly configured.
File Integrity Monitoring: Implement file integrity monitoring to detect unauthorized changes to system files and configurations.
Network Segmentation: Segment networks to limit the spread of malware and restrict lateral movement.
Endpoint Protection: Deploy advanced endpoint protection solutions like Check Point Harmony Endpoint and Threat Emulation.
User Activity Monitoring: Monitor logged-in users and their activities to detect any unauthorized access.
Regular Updates: Keep all systems and software updated with the latest security patches.

Audit System Configurations: Regularly check system configurations and service status.
Ensure services like `rc.local`, `init.d` scripts, and other startup scripts are correctly configured and not tampered with.
Implement File Integrity Monitoring: Use tools like Tripwire or AIDE to monitor critical system files for unauthorized changes.
Set up alerts for any changes to `/etc/rc.local`, `/etc/init.d/`, and other critical files.
Network Segmentation: Create network segments for different parts of the organization.
Implement strict access controls between segments.
Deploy Advanced Endpoint Protection: Install and configure Check Point Harmony Endpoint across all endpoints.
Enable Threat Emulation to detect and block advanced threats.
Monitor User Activity: Set up logging and monitoring tools to track user logins and activities.
Use SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) solutions to correlate and analyze user activities.
Regular System Updates: Schedule regular updates for all systems and applications.
Ensure that security patches are applied promptly.

Detection Signature.Signature name: Unauthorized changes to system startup scripts

Internal checks.Setting2: Monitor creation and modification of files in `/etc/init.d/`.
Internal checks.Setting3: Check for unauthorized processes masquerading as system services (e.g., `ntfsys`).

Detection Signature.External scanning: Not applicable (focus on internal file and process monitoring)

title: New Details on TinyTurla’s Post-Compromise Activity Reveal Full Kill Chain
content:
#### Description
Cisco Talos and CERT.NGO have provided updates on an ongoing campaign by the Russian espionage group, Turla (tracked by Microsoft as Secret Blizzard), revealing the entire kill chain used by the group, including tactics like stealing information and spreading through infected networks. The attackers targeted a European NGO, infecting multiple systems, establishing persistence, and evading anti-virus products before deploying their TinyTurla-NG implant for data exfiltration and network pivoting. Turla's post-compromise activities involve configuring anti-virus exclusions, setting up persistence through batch files, and deploying TinyTurla-NG and a custom Chisel beacon for reconnaissance and exfiltration. Despite initial compromise dates in October 2023, the majority of data exfiltration occurred in January 2024, highlighting the persistence and stealth of Turla's operations.

> [Check out Microsoft's write-up on Secret Blizzard here.](https://sip.security.microsoft.com/intel-profiles/01d15f655c45c517f52235d63932fb377c319176239426681412afb01bf39dcc?)

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/tinyturla-full-kill-chain/


#### Publication Date
March 21, 2024

#### Author(s)
Asheer Malhotra
Holger Unterbrink
Vitor Ventura
Arnaud Zobec

enhanced.Incident: TinyTurla Post-Compromise Activity
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause of the incident was the initial compromise of systems within a European non-governmental organization's network by the Turla espionage group. They exploited the systems by adding exclusions to antivirus software like *Microsoft Defender* (https://gbhackers.com/tinyturla-evolved-ttps-stealth-attacks), establishing persistence via malicious services, and using tools like TinyTurla-NG, *Chisel open-source attack framework* (https://duo.com/decipher/tinyturla-ng-backdoor-has-big-capabilities), batch files for service creation, and PowerShell commands. The attackers engaged in data exfiltration and *credential harvesting* (https://duo.com/decipher/tinyturla-ng-backdoor-has-big-capabilities).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Turla (Russian espionage group) in coordination with *Cisco Talos* (https://gbhackers.com/tinyturla-evolved-ttps-stealth-attacks)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: *European non-governmental organization (NGO) in collaboration with CERT.NGO* (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/tinyturla-ng-tooling-and-c2/)
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: October 2023 – January 2024
MITRE TTPs: T1562.001: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
T1543.003: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
enhanced.Impact: Multiple systems within the NGO's network were compromised, leading to data exfiltration and potential exposure of sensitive information.
Mitigation: Regularly update antivirus and endpoint protection solutions to detect and block known malware.
Implement strict access controls and network segmentation to limit lateral movement.
Monitor and audit registry changes, especially those related to antivirus exclusions and service creation.
Use behavioral analytics to detect anomalous activities such as unauthorized service creation or unexpected network traffic.
Deploy multi-factor authentication (MFA) to secure access to sensitive systems.
Conduct regular security training and awareness programs for employees.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: **Update Antivirus**: Ensure antivirus definitions and endpoint protection software are up-to-date to detect known threats.
**Access Controls**: Implement role-based access controls and network segmentation to limit access to critical systems.
**Registry Monitoring**: Use tools to monitor and audit registry changes, focusing on keys related to antivirus exclusions and service creation.
**Behavioral Analytics**: Deploy solutions that analyze user and system behavior to detect anomalies.
**MFA Deployment**: Implement multi-factor authentication for accessing sensitive systems and data.
**Security Training**: Regularly train employees on security best practices and phishing awareness.

Detection Signature.Signature name: “Windows Defender Exclusions Modified” & “Unauthorized Windows Service Creation”

Internal checks.Setting1: Monitor registry key `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths` for unauthorized exclusions – In platform
Internal checks.Setting2: Monitor registry key `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\services` for unauthorized service creation – Inside VMs
Internal checks.Setting3: Conduct regular audits of service creation and configuration – Inside VMs

title: Analysis of a New MacOS Trojan-Proxy
content:
#### Description
Kaspersky researchers have discovered a new Trojan-Proxy that is piggybacking on cracked software for macOS. he infected versions of the software come in the form of .PKG installers, which are handled by the Installer utility in macOS and can run scripts before and after actual installation.

The Trojan creates log files and attempts to obtain a C&C server IP address via DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), thus making the DNS request indistinguishable from a regular HTTPS request and hiding it from traffic monitoring. The Trojan can be used to build a proxy server network or to perform criminal acts on behalf of the victim, such as launching attacks on websites, companies, and individuals, or buying illicit goods. In addition to the macOS application, Kaspersky researchers discovered several specimens for Android and Windows that connected to the same C&C server. These are also Trojan-Proxies that hide inside cracked software.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://securelist.com/trojan-proxy-for-macos/111325/

#### Publication Date
December 6, 2023

#### Author(s)
Sergey Puzan

enhanced.Incident: New macOS Trojan-Proxy piggybacking on cracked software.
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident is the distribution of cracked software from unauthorized websites, which includes a malicious post-installation script that installs a Trojan-Proxy. This Trojan utilizes the macOS Installer utility to execute scripts that replace legitimate system files with malicious ones. The malware, *Activator.app, uses a Python 3.9.6 installer* and an obsolete function, AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges, to gain admin privileges (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-malware-targets-cracked-apps/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Not specified in the document.

title: Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) Exploiting JetBrains TeamCity CVE Globally
content:
#### Description
Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) cyber actors—also known as Advanced Persistent Threat 29 (APT 29), the Dukes, CozyBear, and NOBELIUM/Midnight Blizzard—are exploiting CVE-2023-42793 at a large scale, targeting servers hosting JetBrains TeamCity software since September 2023.

Software developers use TeamCity software to manage and automate software compilation, building, testing, and releasing. If compromised, access to a TeamCity server would provide malicious actors with access to that software developer’s source code, signing certificates, and the ability to subvert software compilation and deployment processes—access a malicious actor could further use to conduct supply chain operations. Although the SVR used such access to compromise SolarWinds and its customers in 2020, limited number and seemingly opportunistic types of victims currently identified, indicate that the SVR has not used the access afforded by the TeamCity CVE in a similar manner. The SVR has, however, been observed using the initial access gleaned by exploiting the TeamCity CVE to escalate its privileges, move laterally, deploy additional backdoors, and take other steps to ensure persistent and long-term access to the compromised network environments.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-347a

#### Publication Date
December 12, 2023

#### Author(s)
CISA

enhanced.Incident: Shanghai Police Datalake Leak
enhanced.Root cause: Misconfigured JetBrains TeamCity instance, specifically the exploitation of CVE-2023-42793, which allows unauthorized access and code execution on vulnerable servers. *The changes* (https://www.safebreach.com/blog/jetbrains-teamcity-safebreach-coverage-for-us-cert-alert-aa23-347a/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), also known as APT 29, the Dukes, CozyBear, and NOBELIUM/Midnight Blizzard, exploiting CVE-2023-42793 at a large scale since September 2023. *The changes* (https://rhisac.org/threat-intelligence/russian-foreign-intelligence-service-svr-cyber-actors-use-jetbrains-teamcity-cve-in-global-targeting/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Various organizations globally including software developers, IT companies, critical infrastructure, and government agencies in the U.S., Poland, and the U.K., also targeting retail organizations. *The changes* (https://rhisac.org/threat-intelligence/russian-foreign-intelligence-service-svr-cyber-actors-use-jetbrains-teamcity-cve-in-global-targeting/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The exploitation campaign began in late September 2023 and continued into December 2023 when the report was released.

T1592.002: Gather Victim Host Information: Software
T1555.003: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers

enhanced.Impact: A few dozen companies compromised, over a hundred devices impacted, including those of an energy trade association. *The changes* (https://therecord.media/russia-svr-exploiting-jetbrains-vulnerability). Software supply chain compromise poses significant risks. *The changes* (https://rhisac.org/threat-intelligence/russian-foreign-intelligence-service-svr-cyber-actors-use-jetbrains-teamcity-cve-in-global-targeting/).
Mitigation: Apply patches for CVE-2023-42793 issued by JetBrains TeamCity. *The changes* (https://www.safebreach.com/blog/jetbrains-teamcity-safebreach-coverage-for-us-cert-alert-aa23-347a/).
Monitor networks for encoded commands and execution of network scanning tools.
Enable and alert on host-based anti-virus/endpoint monitoring solutions.
Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all services.
Keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date.
Audit log files for access attempts to privileged certificates and creation of fake identity providers.
Deploy software to identify suspicious behavior on systems.
Use public resources to identify credential abuse in cloud environments.
Configure authentication mechanisms to confirm user activities on systems.

Internal Checks: Ensure TeamCity port (8111) is not exposed on the external Internet.
Verify TeamCity instances are secured with authentication credentials.

Additional Information: SVR hackers used VaporRage malware. *The changes* (https://therecord.media/russia-svr-exploiting-jetbrains-vulnerability).
The SVR is involved in Diplomatic Orbiter campaign targeting diplomatic agencies globally. *The changes* (https://therecord.media/russia-svr-exploiting-jetbrains-vulnerability).
*Helga Labus, Managing Editor*, Help Net Security. *The changes* (https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2023/12/14/russian-hackers-cve-2023-42793/).
*Shadowserver Foundation* revealed nearly 800 unpatched instances. *The changes* (https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2023/12/14/russian-hackers-cve-2023-42793/).

title: Known Indicators of Compromise Associated with Androxgh0st Malware
content:
#### Description
Androxgh0st malware has been observed establishing a botnet for victim identification and exploitation in target networks. According to open source reporting, Androxgh0st is a Python-scripted malware primarily used to target .env files that contain confidential information, such as credentials for various high profile applications (i.e., Amazon Web Services [AWS], Microsoft Office 365, SendGrid, and Twilio from the Laravel web application framework). Androxgh0st malware also supports numerous functions capable of abusing the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), such as scanning and exploiting exposed credentials and application programming interfaces (APIs), and web shell deployment.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-016a

#### Publication Date
January 12, 2024

#### Author(s)
CISA

enhanced.Incident: Androxgh0st Malware Campaign
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause includes multiple vulnerabilities such as exposed `.env` files containing credentials, exploitation of `CVE-2017-9841` in PHPUnit allowing remote code execution, *CVE-2018-15133 in Laravel for remote code execution* (https://heimdalsecurity.com/blog/androxgh0st-malware-iocs-and-ttps/), `CVE-2021-41773` in Apache HTTP Server allowing unauthorized access, running outdated and vulnerable versions of Apache HTTP Server (versions 2.4.49 or 2.4.50), and misconfigured server settings that expose sensitive URIs *Your changes* (https://thehackernews.com/2024/03/androxgh0st-malware-targets-laravel.html).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Androxgh0st malware campaign
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Not specified, but the advisory targets general organizations and network defenders.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Ongoing as of the release date of January 16, 2024

MITRE TTPs.Resource Development: Acquire Infrastructure: Botnet [T1583.005], Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services [T1583.006]
MITRE TTPs.Persistence: Valid Accounts [T1078], Server Software Component: Web Shell [T1505.003], Create Account [T1136]
MITRE TTPs.Defense Evasion: Obfuscated Files or Information: Command Obfuscation [T1027.010]
MITRE TTPs.Credential Access: Credential Access [TA0006], Unsecured Credentials: Credentials in Files [T1552.001]
MITRE TTPs.Discovery: File and Directory Discovery [T1083], Network Service Discovery [T1046]

enhanced.Impact: The advisory does not specify the number of records leaked or financial losses. However, the impact includes potential unauthorized access to sensitive data, deployment of web shells, creation of new accounts for malicious purposes, and exploitation for cryptocurrency mining *Your changes* (https://www.checkpoint.com/cyber-hub/threat-prevention/what-is-malware/androxgh0st-malware-everything-you-need-to-know/).

Mitigation.Keep software updated: Ensure all operating systems, software, and firmware are up to date. Specifically, ensure Apache servers are not running versions 2.4.49 or 2.4.50.
Mitigation.Default URI configuration: Verify that the default configuration for all URIs is to deny all requests unless necessary.
Mitigation.Disable Laravel debug mode: Ensure live Laravel applications are not in “debug” or testing mode. Remove and revoke all cloud credentials from `.env` files.
Mitigation.Review and monitor credentials: Regularly review platforms or services for unauthorized access or use of credentials listed in `.env` files.
Mitigation.File system scanning: Scan the server’s file system for unrecognized PHP files, particularly in the root directory or `/vendor/phpunit/phpunit/src/Util/PHP` folder.
Mitigation.Monitor outgoing GET requests: Review outgoing GET requests to file hosting sites like GitHub and pastebin, especially when they access `.php` files.

URIs observed: Many more as listed in the advisory.

Additional Information.AndroxGh0st malware: Primarily targets `.env` files in Laravel applications containing credentials for AWS, O365, SendGrid, and Twilio. It is actively used in the wild and observed by FortiGuard Labs more than 40,000 times a day. Androxgh0st is Python-based, exploits SMTP, and is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities *Your changes* (https://www.checkpoint.com/cyber-hub/threat-prevention/what-is-malware/androxgh0st-malware-everything-you-need-to-know/). Additionally, the malware has been detected leveraging `CVE-2021-41773`, observed by Juniper Threat Labs, and primarily targeting regions including the U.S., U.K., and China. Threat actors also exploit compromised systems for cryptocurrency mining, participation in the Meson Network *Your changes* (https://thehackernews.com/2024/03/androxgh0st-malware-targets-laravel.html). *CISA and FBI advisory recommends timely patching* (https://heimdalsecurity.com/blog/androxgh0st-malware-iocs-and-ttps/). *Juniper Threat Labs identified functions `awslimitcheck`, `sendgridcheck`, and `twillio_sender` for AWS, SendGrid, and Twilio account details extraction* (https://blogs.juniper.net/en-us/security/shielding-networks-against-androxgh0st).

title: Analysis of Nood RAT Used in Attacks Against Linux (Gh0st RATs Variant)
content:
#### Description
AhnLab Security Intelligence Center (ASEC) has discovered that Nood RAT, a variant of Gh0st RAT that works in Linux, is being used in malware attacks. Nood RAT is a backdoor malware that can receive commands from the C&C server to perform malicious activities such as downloading malicious files, stealing systems’ internal files, and executing commands. Although simple in form, it is equipped with an encryption feature to avoid network packet detection.

Nood RAT is developed using a builder that allows the threat actor to create x86 or x64 binary based on the architecture and choose and use the binary that fits the target system. The malware has a feature that changes its name in order to disguise itself as a legitimate program. The threat actor is able to decide the malware’s fake process name during the development stage.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/62144/

#### Publication Date
February 25, 2024

#### Author(s)
Sanseo

enhanced.Incident: Noodle RAT Used in Attacks Against Linux (Gh0st RAT’s Variant)
enhanced.Root cause: Exploitation of vulnerabilities in software such as WebLogic (CVE-2017-10271), weak configuration practices, and possibly insecure AWS server setups.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Likely Chinese-speaking threat actors, potentially including the Rocke group and participants in the Cloud Snooper APT campaign. *Trend Micro identified this as a new malware strain* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-noodle-rat-backdoor/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Multiple organizations across various countries including China, Russia, Hong Kong, Philippines, Vietnam, South Korea, *Thailand, India, Japan, Malaysia, and Taiwan* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-noodle-rat-backdoor/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Ongoing since at least 2018.
MITRE TTPs: T1070.004 (Indicator Removal on Host: File Deletion)
enhanced.Impact: Multiple organizations impacted with varying degrees of data exfiltration and system compromise. Specific financial losses are not detailed.
enhanced.Mitigation: Secure Linux systems by updating to the latest versions and patching known vulnerabilities, particularly WebLogic (CVE-2017-10271). Implement strong authentication mechanisms and access controls to prevent unauthorized access to systems. Monitor and restrict outbound traffic to detect and prevent communication with malicious C&C servers. Use security solutions that can detect and block Nood RAT and its variants (e.g., update antivirus signatures). Regularly review and audit system configurations and credentials to ensure they follow security best practices.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: Patch Management: Regularly apply security patches for all software and systems. Specifically, address vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-10271 in WebLogic.
Access Controls: Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) on all critical systems. Limit the use of administrative privileges and ensure accounts are configured with the least privilege principle.
Network Security: Configure firewalls to block known malicious IP addresses and domains listed in IoCs. Monitor network traffic for unusual activity, such as communication with C&C servers.
Endpoint Protection: Deploy and regularly update endpoint security solutions capable of detecting Nood RAT. Utilize behavioral analysis tools to identify and mitigate suspicious activities.
Incident Response: Develop and test an incident response plan to quickly address and mitigate infections. Train staff to recognize and respond to indicators of compromise.
Backup and Recovery: Maintain regular backups of critical data and ensure that backups are stored securely and tested for integrity.

Internal checks: Setting1: Ensure MySQL and MS-SQL servers are not exposed to the external Internet.
Setting2: Implement strict firewall rules to restrict access to MySQL (3306) and MS-SQL (1433) ports.
Setting3: Secure MySQL and MS-SQL with strong authentication credentials and regular audits.
External scanning: Port (3306, 1433) open
Unusual outbound traffic to known malicious IPs/domains.

enhanced.Additional Information: Noodle RAT exists in two versions: *Win.NOODLERAT and Linux.NOODLERAT* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-noodle-rat-backdoor/). The malware has been misclassified for years but was identified by *Trend Micro* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-noodle-rat-backdoor/). *Virus Total uploads in 2024 confirm its active use* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-noodle-rat-backdoor/).

title: Bumblebee Buzzes Back in Black   Proofpoint US
content:
#### Description
Proofpoint researchers discovered the return of the Bumblebee malware on February 8, 2024, marking its reappearance after four months of absence from their threat data. 

Bumblebee, a sophisticated downloader utilized by various cybercriminal groups, resurfaced in a campaign targeting US organizations through emails with OneDrive URLs containing Word files posing as voicemail messages from "info@quarlesaa[.]com". These Word documents, impersonating the electronics company Humane, utilized macros to execute scripts and download malicious payloads from remote servers. The attack chain, notably employing VBA macro-enabled documents, contrasts with recent trends in cyber threats, where such macros were less commonly used. Despite the absence of attribution to a specific threat actor, Proofpoint warns of Bumblebee's potential as an initial access point for subsequent ransomware attacks. The resurgence of Bumblebee aligns with a broader trend of increased cybercriminal activity observed in 2024, marked by the return of several threat actors and malware strains after prolonged periods of dormancy, indicating a surge in cyber threats following a temporary decline.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/bumblebee-buzzes-back-black

#### Publication Date
February 12, 2024

#### Author(s)
Axel F  
Selena Larson  
Proofpoint Threat Research Team

enhanced.Incident: Bumblebee Buzzes Back in Black
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident involves the use of malicious Word documents with VBA macros. These macros create a script in the Windows temporary directory and execute it using 'wscript'. The script then downloads and executes additional malicious payloads, including the Bumblebee malware, which acts as an initial access broker. *The changes* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/bumblebee-malware-new-attack/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The activity is not attributed to a specific threat actor by Proofpoint at this time. However, the tactics align with previous activities by TA579, and are believed to involve the Conti and TrickBot syndicate. The latest campaign targeted organizations with the subject 'Voicemail February' and spoofed a consumer electronics company called Humane. *The changes* (https://securityboulevard.com/2024/02/bumblebee-malware-targets-us-businesses-with-new-methods/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The campaign targeted organizations in the United States, leveraging AWS Simple Notification Service (SNS) in its tactics. *The changes* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/return-of-bumblebee-and-pikabot-malware-spammers-hit-aws-sns-cyber-threat-intelligence-roundup/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The attack was observed starting on February 8, 2024, after a four-month hiatus. *The changes* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/return-of-bumblebee-and-pikabot-malware-spammers-hit-aws-sns-cyber-threat-intelligence-roundup/).
MITRE TTPs: T1059.001: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
enhanced.Impact: The specific number of impacted records or devices is not provided in the blog, but the campaign involved several thousand emails targeting organizations in the United States. Each email contained OneDrive URLs leading to the malicious Word document. *The changes* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/return-of-bumblebee-and-pikabot-malware-spammers-hit-aws-sns-cyber-threat-intelligence-roundup/).
Mitigation: Disable macros in Microsoft Office files by default to prevent automatic execution of malicious scripts.
Use email security solutions to detect and block phishing emails containing malicious URLs or attachments.
Educate users on recognizing phishing emails and avoiding clicking on suspicious links or downloading unsolicited attachments.
Implement robust endpoint protection solutions that can detect and block malicious scripts and PowerShell commands.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: Disable VBA Macros by Default: In Office 365 Admin Center, configure the 'Macro Settings' in the 'Trust Center' to disable macros by default and only allow signed macros.
Email Security: Deploy advanced email security solutions that use machine learning to detect and block phishing emails. Implement URL filtering to block access to known malicious sites.
User Education: Conduct regular security awareness training for employees to recognize phishing attempts. Simulate phishing attacks to test and improve employee vigilance.

Endpoint Protection: Deploy endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions that can monitor and block suspicious activities like script execution and unauthorized PowerShell commands. Ensure antivirus software is up-to-date and capable of detecting the latest malware signatures.

Internal checks: Setting1: Macros should be disabled by default in all Microsoft Office applications. – In platform
Setting2: Enable logging for macro execution and monitor for suspicious activities. – Inside VMs
Setting3: Use endpoint protection to detect and block malicious script execution. – Inside VMs
External scanning: Scan email traffic for known malicious URLs and attachments.
Monitor network traffic for connections to known malicious domains and IP addresses.

title: URL files and WebDAV used for IcedID (Bokbot) infection, (Fri, Feb 24th)
content:
#### Description
IcedID (also known as Bokbot) is an information stealer/backdoor malware that can lead to other activity like Cobalt Strike and Virtual Network Computing (VNC) traffic. IcedID is often distributed through email, and it has also been delivered by fake software sites from Google ad traffic. Recently, distribution was done from using .url files that were likely attached to an email. On Tuesday 2023-02-21, @wwp96 [tweeted](https://twitter.com/wwp96/status/1628126394487300096) about an open directory at **_hxxp\[:\]//104.156.149\[.\]6/webdav/_**.  Searching VirusTotal revealed at least 22 .url files that attempted to contact the server.  These .url files all use file:\\\\ instead of http:// for the URL and they all grab a similarly-named .bat file from the open directory. The .bat file runs a DLL installer named **_host.dll_** for IcedID on the same server. The .url and .bat files both use WebDAV to retrieve and run the malware.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://isc.sans.edu/diary/rss/29578
2. https://twitter.com/wwp96/status/1628126394487300096


#### Publication Date
February 23, 2023

#### Author(s)
Brad Duncan

enhanced.Incident: URL files and WebDAV used for IcedID (Bokbot) infection
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause involves the usage of Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) services to host and distribute malicious payloads via .url and .bat files, initiating the infection process.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The campaign is linked to IcedID (Bokbot) malware, an information stealer and backdoor often associated with Cobalt Strike and VNC traffic. *IcedID is often distributed through email and fake software sites from Google ad traffic. OneNote files were used as an initial lure this month* (https://isc.sans.edu/diary/29578). *It uses a proxy server and ATS Engine for its operations; it is also known to be dropped by Emotet* (https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/white-papers/security-primer-icedid#:~:text=IcedID%2C%20also%20known%20as%20BokBot,credentials%20for%20online%20banking%20sessions.).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Not specified in the document.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The infection pattern was discovered on 2023-02-21, and the specific infection analyzed was generated on 2023-02-23. *@wwp96 tweeted about an open directory at hxxp://104.156.149[.]6/webdav/* (https://isc.sans.edu/diary/29578).
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
enhanced.Impact: Multiple .url files contacting a malicious WebDAV server, leading to potential widespread infection by IcedID malware.
Mitigation: Configure WebDAV securely: Ensure WebDAV services are properly configured and secured to prevent unauthorized access.
Network Segmentation: Isolate WebDAV servers from critical infrastructure to limit the impact of any compromise.
Email Filtering: Implement advanced email filtering to detect and block emails containing malicious .url or .bat files.
Endpoint Protection: Deploy and maintain up-to-date endpoint protection solutions capable of detecting and preventing IcedID malware.
User Education: Educate users about the dangers of opening unsolicited email attachments and links.
Monitor Network Traffic: Implement network monitoring to detect unusual WebDAV traffic patterns.
Detailed Steps for Mitigation: Secure WebDAV: Disable WebDAV if not necessary. Use strong authentication mechanisms (e.g., Basic or Digest authentication over HTTPS). Regularly update WebDAV software to patch known vulnerabilities.
Email Filtering: Set up rules to block .url and .bat file attachments. Use sandbox environments to analyze suspicious email attachments.
Endpoint Protection: Ensure antivirus/antimalware tools are configured to scan all file types, including .url and .bat. Enable real-time protection and automatic updates.

Network Monitoring: Set up intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS) to monitor for WebDAV-specific traffic, such as HTTP PROPFIND requests. Utilize SIEM tools to correlate and analyze network traffic patterns.

Internal checks.Setting1: WebDAV service should not be accessible externally without proper authorization.
Internal checks.Setting2: Monitor for unusual HTTP PROPFIND requests indicative of WebDAV usage.
Internal checks.Setting3: Ensure WebDAV services require authentication credentials.

IoCs: Other IoCs: IP Address: 104.156.149[.]6, Domain: mandalorecnote[.]com, Domain: ituitem[.]net, Domain: renomesolar[.]com, Domain: palasedelareforma[.]com, Domain: noosaerty[.]com. *Decoy traffic to mandalorecnote[.]com/images/* (https://isc.sans.edu/diary/29578)
enhanced.Additional Information: *DDoS-as-a-Service is a new threat where cybercriminals offer their expertise for large-scale attacks, including DDoS extortion attacks for financial gain, primarily affecting the financial services sector* (https://www.deepwatch.com/labs/cyber-intel-brief-feb-23-mar-01-2023/)

title: BB17 distribution Qakbot (Qbot) activity
content:
#### Description

#### Reference URL(s)

2. https://www.virustotal.com/gui/url/f1cd5c2c1f1d80c9758a55d26c1124a199eda9d026cec686a20a0df67131cc31
