title: AA23-025A Protecting Against Malicious Use of Remote Monitoring and Management Software
content:
#### Description
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), National Security Agency (NSA), and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) are releasing this joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) to warn network defenders about malicious use of legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. 

In October 2022, CISA identified a widespread cyber campaign involving the malicious use of legitimate RMM software. Specifically, cyber criminal actors sent phishing emails that led to the download of legitimate RMM software—ScreenConnect (now ConnectWise Control) and AnyDesk—which the actors used in a refund scam to steal money from victim bank accounts.

Although this campaign appears financially motivated, the authoring organizations assess it could lead to additional types of malicious activity. For example, the actors could sell victim account access to other cyber criminal or advanced persistent threat (APT) actors. This campaign highlights the threat of malicious cyber activity associated with legitimate RMM software: after gaining access to the target network via phishing or other techniques, malicious cyber actors—from cybercriminals to nation-state sponsored APTs—are known to use legitimate RMM software as a backdoor for persistence and/or command and control (C2).

Using portable executables of RMM software provides a way for actors to establish local user access without the need for administrative privilege and full software installation—effectively bypassing common software controls and risk management assumptions.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa23-025a

#### Publication Date
January 25, 2023

#### Author(s)
CISA

enhanced.markdown:
Incident: Malicious Use of Remote Monitoring and Management Software

Root cause: The incident was caused by cybercriminals using legitimate Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) software, specifically ScreenConnect (now ConnectWise Control) and AnyDesk, to gain unauthorized access to victim systems. This was facilitated through a phishing campaign tricking victims into downloading and executing the RMM software.

Threat Actor/group/campaign: Cybercriminal actors; potentially selling access to other cybercriminals or advanced persistent threat (APT) actors.

Organization/industry/location: Federal civilian executive branch (FCEB) networks and potentially other victims targeted through phishing campaigns. *The National Security Agency (NSA) and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) are also involved* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/cisa-warns-malicious-use-rmm/).

Start date – End date: Since at least June 2022; identified in October 2022.

*Technical Details*: In June 2022, EINSTEIN IDS identified suspected malicious activity on two FCEB networks *using trusted third-party reporting* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-025a).

MITRE TTPs:
- T1078: Valid Accounts
- T1071: Application Layer Protocol
- T1219: Remote Access Software

Impact: Financial losses due to refund scams, potential unauthorized access to sensitive information, and potential misuse of victim accounts.

Mitigation:
- Implement best practices to block phishing emails.
- Audit remote access tools on your network to identify authorized RMM software.
- Review logs for execution of RMM software to detect abnormal use.
- Use security software to detect instances of RMM software only being loaded in memory.
- Implement application controls to manage and control execution of software, including allowlisting RMM programs.
- Require authorized RMM solutions to be used from within your network over approved remote access solutions, such as VPNs or VDIs.
- Block both inbound and outbound connections on common RMM ports and protocols at the network perimeter.
- Implement a user training program and phishing exercises to raise awareness among users about the risks of visiting suspicious websites, clicking on suspicious links, and opening suspicious attachments. *Alessandro Mascellino emphasized the need for stronger anti-phishing controls and cybersecurity awareness* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/cisa-warns-malicious-use-rmm/).

Detection Signature:
Service: ScreenConnect (now ConnectWise Control), AnyDesk
Port: Varies based on configuration
Severity: Critical
Incident: Malicious Use of RMM Software
Signature name: “Unauthorized RMM Software Execution”
Internal checks:
- Setting1: Audit for unauthorized RMM software on endpoints.
- Setting2: Monitor for execution of portable executables that match known RMM software.
- Setting3: Ensure RMM software usage is within policy and only executed from authorized sources.
External scanning:
- Port scanning for common RMM software ports.
- Detection of anomalous RMM software usage patterns.

IoCs:
- win03[.]xyz
- myhelpcare[.]online (observed on June 14, 2022)
- win01[.]xyz
- myhelpcare[.]cc
- 247secure[.]us

*Note*: Portable executables bypass controls and risk management assumptions by not requiring administrative privileges *(https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-025a)*.

*Additional Context*: Silent Push identified related malicious typosquatting activity involving Amazon, Microsoft, Geek Squad, McAfee, Norton, and PayPal domains *(https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-025a)*. *Mike Walters from Action1 highlighted detecting hackers' misuse of RMM solutions* (https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/cisa-warns-malicious-use-rmm/).

title: Vice Society Ransomware Group Targets Manufacturing Companies
content:
#### Description
Vice Society, which was initially reported to be exploiting the PrintNightmare vulnerability in their routines, have previously deployed ransomware variants such as Hello Kitty/Five Hands and Zeppelin (the group’s email has been in their ransom notes). More recently, Vice Society has been able to develop its own custom ransomware builder and adopt more robust encryption methods. This, and any further enhancements, could mean that the group is preparing for their own ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation.

Through Trend Micro’s telemetry data, they have evidence that the group is also targeting the manufacturing sector, which means that Vice Society have capability and desire to penetrate different industries — most likely accomplished via the purchasing of compromised credentials from underground channels. We have detected the presence of Vice Society in Brazil (primarily affecting the country’s manufacturing industry), Argentina, Switzerland, and Israel. 

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/a/vice-society-ransomware-group-targets-manufacturing-companies.html


#### Publication Date
January 25, 2023

#### Author(s)
Ieriz Nicolle Gonzalez  
Paul Pajares  
Arianne Dela Cruz  
Warren Sto.Tomas

enhanced.Incident: Vice Society Ransomware Group Targets Manufacturing Companies and Education Sector *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0).
enhanced.Root Cause: The incident was primarily caused by the exploitation of vulnerable public-facing websites and compromised Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) credentials. This allowed the attackers to gain initial access and further leverage tools like Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz for lateral movement and credential harvesting. Additionally, the group used a custom encryptor named PolyVice, which combines asymmetric encryption with the NTRUEncrypt algorithm and symmetric encryption with the ChaCha20-Poly1305 algorithm *The changes* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/vice-society-ransomware-gang-switches-to-new-custom-encryptor/). The attackers also used phishing and spear phishing emails, PrintNightmare exploitation (CVE-2021-34527 and CVE-2021-1675) *The changes* (https://www.sentinelone.com/anthology/vice-society/), and deployed versions of Hello Kitty/Five Hands and Zeppelin ransomware *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Vice Society Ransomware Group, which emerged in early to mid-2021 *The changes* (https://www.sentinelone.com/anthology/vice-society/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Manufacturing companies in Brazil, Argentina, Switzerland, and Israel were among the targets. Vice Society also targets ESXi or heavily virtualized environments *The changes* (https://www.sentinelone.com/anthology/vice-society/). Additionally, the education sector, especially K-12 institutions, has been disproportionately targeted *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The attacks were observed from late 2022 to early 2023, with significant activity noted between October 28, 2022, and January 2023.
MITRE TTPs: Initial Access: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application), T1078 (Valid Accounts)
Execution: T1059.001 (PowerShell), T1059.003 (Windows Command Shell), T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation) *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0)

Persistence: T1078 (Valid Accounts), Registry RUN key *The changes* (https://www.sentinelone.com/anthology/vice-society/), T1547.001 (Registry Run Keys/Startup Folder), T1574.002 (DLL Side-Loading) *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0)
Privilege Escalation: T1078 (Valid Accounts), T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation) *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0)

Defense Evasion: T1562.001 (Disable or Modify Tools), T1070.004 (File Deletion), T1070.006 (Timestomp), T1036 (Masquerading) *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0)
Credential Access: T1003 (OS Credential Dumping), T1558.003 (Kerberoasting), T1055 (Process Injection) *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0)
Lateral Movement: T1021.001 (Remote Desktop Protocol), T1080 (Taint Shared Content) *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0)
Command and Control: T1105 (Ingress Tool Transfer)
Exfiltration: T1041 (Exfiltration Over C2 Channel), TA0010 (Exfiltration for double extortion) *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0)
Impact: T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact), T1531 (Account Access Removal) *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0)
enhanced.Impact: Numerous companies across multiple industries were affected, with significant data exfiltration and operational disruption. Financial losses and data recovery costs could be substantial.

Immediate Steps: Ensure all public-facing applications are updated and patched.
Implement strong password policies and multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Regularly update and patch all systems and software.
Conduct regular security awareness training for employees.
Long-term Steps: Deploy endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions.
Use network segmentation to limit lateral movement.
Implement robust backup solutions and regularly test backups.
Monitor network and endpoint activities for suspicious behavior.
Establish and maintain strong liaison relationships with the FBI Field Office and CISA regional offices *The changes* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa22-249a-0).

Internal Checks: Setting1: RDP port (3389) should not be exposed on the external Internet. – In platform
Setting2: RDP port (3389) should not listen on the external Internet – Inside VMs
Setting3: RDP server should secure with authentication credentials. – Inside VMs

enhanced.Note: Further details and a full list of IoCs can be found in the linked text file provided in the blog.
enhanced.IoCs found: Yes, they are provided in the blog, including domains, email addresses, and file paths.

title: Chinese Entanglement  DLL Hijacking in the Asian Gambling Sector
content:
#### Description
SentinelLabs has identified suspected-Chinese malware and infrastructure potentially involved in China-associated operations directed at the gambling sector within Southeast Asia.  The threat actors abuse Adobe Creative Cloud, Microsoft Edge, and McAfee VirusScan executables vulnerable to DLL hijacking to deploy Cobalt Strike beacons.

SentinelLabs observed related malware using the signature of a likely stolen code signing certificate issued to PMG PTE LTD, a Singapore-based vendor of Ivacy VPN services.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/chinese-entanglement-dll-hijacking-in-the-asian-gambling-sector/


#### Publication Date
August 17, 2023

#### Author(s)
Aleksandar Milenkoski

enhanced.Incident: Chinese Entanglement | DLL Hijacking in the Asian Gambling Sector
enhanced.Root cause: The incident involved vulnerable executables (Adobe Creative Cloud, Microsoft Edge, McAfee VirusScan) prone to DLL hijacking, aiding the deployment of Cobalt Strike beacons. The compromise of a code-signing certificate issued to PMG PTE LTD facilitated the attack. *The deployment of the HUI Loader to load remote access trojans and ransomware like LockFile and AtomSilo played a crucial role* (https://www.secureworks.com/research/bronze-starlight-ransomware-operations-use-hui-loader). *The hackers also exploited a stolen Ivacy VPN certificate to bypass security measures* (https://blog.koddos.net/chinese-hacker-group-targets-southeast-asian-gambling-industry-using-stolen-ivacy-vpn-certificate/). *Earth Freybug utilized UNAPIMON malware for stealthy operations* (https://thehackernews.com/search/label/DLL%20hijacking). *Additionally, BluetoothDiagnosticUtil.dll was used to launch the final payload* (https://thehackernews.com/search/label/DLL%20hijacking).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The China-aligned BRONZE STARLIGHT group, also known as DEV-0401 or SLIME34, executed the attack, with potential involvement of interconnected Chinese APT groups. *BRONZE RIVERSIDE also appears to be linked to similar activities* (https://www.secureworks.com/research/bronze-starlight-ransomware-operations-use-hui-loader). *The campaign is part of Operation ChattyGoblin* (https://blog.koddos.net/chinese-hacker-group-targets-southeast-asian-gambling-industry-using-stolen-ivacy-vpn-certificate/). *Earth Freybug, a subset of APT41, was also active* (https://thehackernews.com/search/label/DLL%20hijacking).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Targeted the gambling sector within Southeast Asia, specifically companies in the Philippines.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Activities observed in March 2023. *The issue dates back to May 29, 2023* (https://blog.koddos.net/chinese-hacker-group-targets-southeast-asian-gambling-industry-using-stolen-ivacy-vpn-certificate/).
enhanced.Impact: The specific number of records leaked or financial losses is not mentioned in the document.
Mitigation: Regularly update and patch all software components to fix known vulnerabilities.
Implement strict code signing policies and monitor for unauthorized use of code-signing certificates.
Employ endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions to detect and mitigate DLL hijacking attempts.
Conduct regular security audits and penetration testing to identify and remediate vulnerabilities.
Use network segmentation to limit the spread of infections.
Monitor network traffic for unusual activity, such as communications with known malicious C2 domains.

Detection Signature.Service: Microsoft Edge, Adobe Creative Cloud, McAfee VirusScan
Detection Signature.Port: N/A (DLL hijacking does not involve specific ports)
Detection Signature.Incident: DLL Hijacking Deployment of Cobalt Strike

Internal checks.Setting1: Ensure all software is updated to the latest versions.
Internal checks.Setting2: Monitor for unauthorized DLLs in directories of critical applications.
Internal checks.Setting3: Implement application whitelisting to prevent unauthorized DLL loading.

title: XLoader’s Latest Trick  New macOS Variant Disguised as Signed OfficeNote App
content:
#### Description
XLoader is a long-running malware-as-a-service infostealer and botnet that has been around in some form or another since 2015. Its first macOS variant was spotted in 2021 and was notable for being distributed as a Java program. 

Now, however, XLoader has returned in a new form and without the dependencies. Written natively in the C and Objective C programming languages and signed with an Apple developer signature, XLoader is now masquerading as an office productivity app called ‘OfficeNote’.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/xloaders-latest-trick-new-macos-variant-disguised-as-signed-officenote-app/

#### Publication Date
August 22, 2023

#### Author(s)
Phil Stokes  
Dinesh Devados

Incident: XLoader macOS Variant Disguise.Root Cause: The root cause of this incident is the distribution of a new variant of the XLoader malware. This variant is written in C and Objective C, signed with a legitimate Apple developer signature, and masquerades as an office productivity app called 'OfficeNote'. The malware gains persistence by dropping a LaunchAgent and creating a hidden directory with a minimal app. The malware can also be distributed as a .jar file requiring Java Runtime Environment for execution (https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/detecting-xloader-a-macos-malware-as-a-service-info-stealer-and-keylogger/). It leverages social engineering tactics to entice users into downloading and executing the malicious app (https://smartermsp.com/cybersecurity-threat-advisory-xloader-malware-targeting-macos/). *The malware is packaged in a dmg file and delivered with a valid Apple developer signature intact* (https://cymulate.com/blog/cyber-threat-breakdown-august-2023/).
Incident: XLoader macOS Variant Disguise.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The specific threat actor behind this campaign is not mentioned in the report. However, XLoader is known to be a malware-as-a-service infostealer and botnet. *Lazarus Group utilizes CollectionRAT for persistence* (https://www.keysight.com/blogs/en/tech/nwvs/2023/09/14/threat-simulator-august-2023-update).
Incident: XLoader macOS Variant Disguise.Organization/industry/location: Any macOS user or business, particularly those in a working environment, could be targeted.
Incident: XLoader macOS Variant Disguise.Start date \u2013 End date: The application's developer signature was signed on July 17, 2023. The blog was published on August 21, 2023, indicating the attack was identified and reported around this time.
MITRE TTPs: T1547.001: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
Incident: XLoader macOS Variant Disguise.Impact: The specific number of records leaked or financial losses is not provided. However, the impact includes the theft of secrets from the clipboard and browser data, which could lead to further compromises. The malware also drops a Windows icon file (NVFFY.ico) in the user's home directory (https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/detecting-xloader-a-macos-malware-as-a-service-info-stealer-and-keylogger/). The malware targets web browsers like Chrome and Firefox (https://smartermsp.com/cybersecurity-threat-advisory-xloader-malware-targeting-macos/). *It also takes screen captures to exfiltrate data for further use* (https://cymulate.com/blog/cyber-threat-breakdown-august-2023/).
Mitigation: Deploy Third-Party Security Solutions: Use endpoint protection platforms that can detect and prevent malware like XLoader.
Monitor Developer Signatures: Regularly check and revoke compromised developer certificates.
User Education: Educate users about the risks of downloading and installing applications from untrusted sources.
Application Control: Implement strict application control policies to prevent unauthorized applications from running.
Regular Updates: Ensure systems and software are regularly updated to the latest versions to benefit from the latest security protections.
Detailed Steps for Mitigation: Update Endpoint Protection: Ensure all macOS devices have updated antivirus and anti-malware solutions.
Revoke Compromised Certificates: Regularly review and revoke any developer certificates that may have been compromised.
User Awareness Training: Conduct regular training sessions for employees to recognize phishing attempts and avoid downloading suspicious files.
Application Whitelisting: Use application whitelisting to allow only approved applications to run on devices.
System Audits: Perform regular system audits to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities.

Internal checks: Check for unauthorized applications named 'OfficeNote'.
Monitor for the presence of suspicious LaunchAgents in the User’s Library folder.
Inspect for hidden directories and randomized executables in user home directories.
Detection Signature.External scanning: Monitor for network communication to known XLoader C2 IP addresses.

title: Stealth Falcon Preying Over Middle Eastern Skies with Deadglyph
content:
#### Description
ESET researchers have discovered a new sophisticated malware named Deadglyph used by the Stealth Falcon APT group for espionage in the Middle East.

Deadglyph has an unusual architecture consisting of cooperating components; one is a native x64 binary, and the other is a .NET assembly. This combination is unusual because malware typically uses only one programming language for its components. The traditional backdoor commands are dynamically received by the backdoor from the command and control (C2) server in the form of additional modules. The backdoor also has a variety of capabilities to avoid detection, such as continuous monitoring of system processes and randomized network patterns.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/stealth-falcon-preying-middle-eastern-skies-deadglyph/

#### Publication Date
September 22, 2023

#### Author(s)
ESET Research

enhanced.Incident: Stealth Falcon preying over Middle Eastern skies with Deadglyph
enhanced.Root cause: Misconfigured systems allowed the deployment of a sophisticated backdoor, Deadglyph, leveraging Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) event subscription for persistence. The backdoor exploits system defense weaknesses using components encrypted with a machine-specific key and obfuscation techniques to avoid detection. *The attack involved a homoglyph attack using Cyrillic 'M' and Greek 'o' in place of Latin characters in 'Microsoft Corporation'* (https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/stealth-falcon-apt-microsoft-homoglyph-attack). *The initial component is a registry shellcode loader, which loads shellcode from the registry. This extracted shellcode, in turn, loads the native x64 part of the backdoor – the Executor. The Executor subsequently loads the .NET part of the backdoor – the Orchestrator* (https://securityaffairs.com/151298/malware/deadglyph-backdoor-middle-east.html). *Distinctive artifacts like '0xDEADB001' were found within Deadglyph* (https://hackread.com/deadglyph-backdoor-stealth-falcon-apt-middle-east/). *Deadglyph can uninstall itself to minimize detection likelihood* (https://version-2.com/en/2023/10/uae-linked-stealth-falcon-spies-with-sophisticated-new-backdoor-on-its-neighbors-eset-research-discovers/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Stealth Falcon (also known as Project Raven or FruityArmor), *utilizing tools like the Karma hacking tool* (https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-spying-raven/). *ESET attributes Deadglyph to UAE* (https://version-2.com/en/2023/10/uae-linked-stealth-falcon-spies-with-sophisticated-new-backdoor-on-its-neighbors-eset-research-discovers/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Governmental entity in the Middle East, specifically targeting entities in Qatar and other Middle Eastern regions. *The attack spanned the Anatolian and Arabian peninsulas* (https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/stealth-falcon-apt-microsoft-homoglyph-attack).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Detected in 2023; specific start and end dates not provided.
MITRE TTPs: T1583.003: Acquire Infrastructure: Virtual Private Server
T1588.003: Obtain Capabilities: Code Signing Certificates
T1059.003: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
T1546.003: Persistence: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
T1027: Defense Evasion: Obfuscated Files or Information
T1218.011: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
T1562.001: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
T1518.001: Software Discovery: Security Software Discovery
T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
enhanced.Impact: Significant espionage and data exfiltration from Middle Eastern governmental entities.
Mitigation: Use endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions to monitor for unusual WMI event subscriptions.
Employ advanced threat detection mechanisms to identify and block obfuscated malware components.
Regularly update and patch systems to mitigate exploitation of known vulnerabilities.
Implement strict access controls and audit logs to monitor for unauthorized registry modifications and process creations.
Use network segmentation to limit C&C server communications and exfiltration pathways.
Deploy endpoint protection solutions capable of detecting reflective code loading and AMSI patching techniques.

Detection Signature.Port: N/A (WMI utilizes various ports, primarily 135 for DCOM)
Internal checks: Monitor for the creation of WMI event subscriptions.
Audit changes to the registry keys associated with WMI event subscriptions.
Monitor for rundll32.exe executions with unusual DLLs.
External scanning: Detect outgoing HTTP(S) traffic to known C&C domains.

Certificate.Subject: RHM LIMITED, St. Albans, Hertfordshire, GB

enhanced.Additional Information: *The operation involved former NSA operatives like Lori Stroud, recruited by a Maryland cybersecurity contractor, to work for the UAE's National Electronic Security Authority (NESA) and DarkMatter* (https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-spying-raven/). *ESET discovered a second sample of the malware uploaded to Virus Total from Qatar* (https://www.darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/stealth-falcon-apt-microsoft-homoglyph-attack). *Deadglyph’s architecture comprises cooperating components, a native x64 binary and other .NET assembly, enhancing its evasion capabilities* (https://securityaffairs.com/151298/malware/deadglyph-backdoor-middle-east.html). *Modules like Process Creator and Info Collector enhance its capabilities* (https://hackread.com/deadglyph-backdoor-stealth-falcon-apt-middle-east/). *A multistage shellcode downloader chain is involved in the installation process* (https://hackread.com/deadglyph-backdoor-stealth-falcon-apt-middle-east/). *Deadglyph features continuous monitoring of system processes and randomized network patterns to avoid detection* (https://version-2.com/en/2023/10/uae-linked-stealth-falcon-spies-with-sophisticated-new-backdoor-on-its-neighbors-eset-research-discovers/).

title: StopRansomware AvosLocker Ransomware (Update)
content:
#### Description
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are releasing this joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) to disseminate known IOCs, TTPs, and detection methods associated with the AvosLocker variant.

AvosLocker operates under a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model. AvosLocker affiliates have compromised organizations across multiple critical infrastructure sectors in the United States, affecting Windows, Linux, and VMware ESXi environments. AvosLocker affiliates compromise organizations’ networks by using legitimate software and open-source remote system administration tools. AvosLocker affiliates then use exfiltration-based data extortion tactics with threats of leaking and/or publishing stolen data.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-284a

#### Publication Date
October 12, 2023

#### Author(s)
CISA

enhanced.Incident: AvosLocker Ransomware Attack
enhanced.Root cause:
The root cause behind the incident is the exploitation of remote access tools and legitimate software by AvosLocker affiliates. The vulnerable/misconfigured services include:
- Remote system administration tools (Splashtop Streamer, Tactical RMM, PuTTy, AnyDesk, PDQ Deploy, Atera Agent)
- Use of custom PowerShell and batch scripts for lateral movement and privilege escalation, and credential harvesting using *Lazagne and Mimikatz* (https://www.hipaajournal.com/cisa-fbi-avoslocker-ransomware-cybersecurity-advisory/)
- Use of legitimate Windows tools (PsExec, Nltest)
- Open-source networking tunneling tools (Ligolo, Chisel)
- Webshells for network access
*Use of adversary emulation frameworks Cobalt Strike and Sliver for command and control* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-shares-avoslocker-ransomware-technical-details-defense-tips/)
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: AvosLocker Ransomware (operating under a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model), engaging in *exfiltration-based extortion* (https://www.hipaajournal.com/cisa-fbi-avoslocker-ransomware-cybersecurity-advisory/)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Multiple critical infrastructure sectors in the United States, including *government, financial services, and critical manufacturing* (https://www.scworld.com/news/fbi-cisa-warn-critical-infrastructure-organizations-about-avoslocker-ransomware)
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Not specified (mentioned as recent as May 2023)
enhanced.MITRE TTPs:
- External Remote Services (T1133)
- Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell (T1059.001)
- Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell (T1059.003)
- Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047)
- Protocol Tunneling (T1572)
- Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)
- Server Software Component: Web Shell (T1505.003)
enhanced.Impact: The exact number of impacted records is not specified, but the ransomware affected organizations across multiple critical infrastructure sectors.
enhanced.Mitigation:
To protect against AvosLocker ransomware, the following steps should be taken: 
1. Secure remote access tools by implementing application controls and allowlisting remote access programs.
2. Strictly limit the use of RDP and other remote desktop services. Apply best practices like closing unused RDP ports, enforcing account lockouts, applying phishing-resistant MFA, and logging RDP login attempts.
3. Disable command-line and scripting activities and permissions.
4. Restrict the use of PowerShell and update it to the latest version. Enable enhanced PowerShell logging.
5. Configure the Windows Registry to require User Account Control (UAC) approval for any PsExec operations.
6. Disable File and Printer sharing services or use strong passwords/Active Directory authentication if required.
7. Implement a recovery plan with multiple offline backups.
8. Require all accounts with password logins to comply with NIST standards for password policies and enforce phishing-resistant multifactor authentication.
9. Keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date, especially patching known exploited vulnerabilities.
10. Segment networks to prevent ransomware spread and use network monitoring tools to detect abnormal activity.
11. Install, regularly update, and enable real-time detection for antivirus software.
12. Disable unused ports and add email banners to emails received from outside the organization.
13. Ensure all backup data is encrypted and immutable.
*14. Implement YARA rules to detect malware disguised as legitimate tools* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-shares-avoslocker-ransomware-technical-details-defense-tips/).
enhanced.Detection Signature:
Service: Remote system administration tools (Splashtop Streamer, Tactical RMM, PuTTy, AnyDesk, PDQ Deploy, Atera Agent)
Port: Multiple (including port 443 for NetMonitor.exe)
Severity: Critical
Incident: AvosLocker Ransomware Attack
Signature name: “Remote Access Tools and Protocol Tunneling”
Internal checks:
- Ensure remote access tools are allowlisted and unauthorized tools are blocked.
- Secure PowerShell usage with group policies and enable enhanced logging.
- Verify that webshells are not present on web servers.
External scanning:
- Scan for open ports commonly used by remote access tools.
- Detect use of protocol tunneling tools like Ligolo and Chisel.
*15. Monitor for the presence of NetMonitor.exe to ensure it is not acting as a reverse proxy* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-shares-avoslocker-ransomware-technical-details-defense-tips/).

title: Arid Viper Disguising Mobile Spyware as Updates for Non-Malicious Android Applications
content:
#### Description
Since April 2022, Cisco Talos has been tracking a malicious campaign operated by the espionage-motivated Arid Viper advanced persistent threat (APT) group targeting Arabic-speaking Android users. In this campaign, the actors leverage custom mobile malware, also known as Android Package files (APKs), to collect sensitive information from targets and deploy additional malware onto infected devices.

The mobile malware used in this campaign shares similarities with a non-malicious online dating application, referred to as Skipped. The malware specifically uses a similar name and the same shared project on the applications’ development platform. This overlap suggests the Arid Viper operators are either linked to Skipped’s developer or somehow gained illicit access to the shared project’s database. Cisco's analysis uncovered an array of simulated dating applications that are linked to Skipped, leading us to assess that Arid Viper operators may seek to leverage these additional applications in future malicious campaigns. In order to coerce users into downloading their mobile malware, Arid Viper operators share malicious links masquerading as updates to the dating applications, that instead deliver malware to the user’s device.

Arid Viper’s Android malware has a number of features that enable the operators to disable security notifications, collect users’ sensitive information, and deploy additional malicious applications on the compromised device.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/arid-viper-mobile-spyware/

#### Publication Date
October 31, 2023

#### Author(s)
Cisco Talos

enhanced.Incident: Arid Viper Mobile Spyware Campaign
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident includes the exploitation of legitimate application names and shared project resources on the Firebase platform to disguise malware as updates for non-malicious Android applications. The attackers leveraged the overlap in Firebase project credentials and API keys to deploy their malicious APKs.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Arid Viper advanced persistent threat (APT) group with *Hamas-aligned interests* (https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/arid-viper-apts-nest-of-spyc23-malware-continues-to-target-android-devices/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Targeted Arabic-speaking Android users, particularly in regions with Arabic-speaking populations and specific areas such as *Egypt and Palestine* (https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/arid-viper-poisons-android-apps-with-aridspy/#:~:text=In%20August%202023%20we%20logged,by%20the%20initial%2C%20trojanized%20app.).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The campaign has been active since at least April 2022.
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol - Web Protocols
T1056.002: Input Capture - GUI Input Capture
T1056.004: Input Capture - Credential API Hooking
enhanced.Impact: Potentially thousands of Android devices affected, with significant data exfiltration including contacts, call logs, SMS messages, and other sensitive information. Financial and personal data security impacts are substantial, but exact numbers are not provided.
Mitigation: Regularly update and patch Android devices and applications.
Avoid downloading applications from unofficial sources or links shared via social media or messaging apps.
Employ endpoint protection solutions such as Cisco Secure Endpoint to detect and block malicious activities.
Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) to add an extra layer of security.
Regularly monitor and review application permissions on Android devices.
Educate users about the risks of downloading applications from untrusted sources.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: Enable automatic updates for Android OS and applications to ensure timely patching.
Install applications only from Google Play Store or other trusted sources.
Regularly review app permissions and restrict unnecessary access.
Use endpoint security solutions to identify and block malware.
Implement network security solutions to monitor and block malicious domains and IPs.

Internal checks.Setting1: Ensure Firebase projects are not accessible in test mode beyond the allowed 30 days.
Internal checks.Setting2: Regularly audit Firebase project credentials and API keys.
Internal checks.Setting3: Monitor for unusual API calls and data transfers within Firebase projects.

External scanning.Monitor for domains associated with know: Detect and alert on unusual traffic patterns to Firebase endpoints.

title: A Deep Dive into Phobos Ransomware, Recently Deployed by 8Base Group
content:
#### Description
Cisco Talos has recently observed an increase in activity conducted by 8Base, a ransomware group that uses a variant of the Phobos ransomware and other publicly available tools to facilitate their operations.

Most of the group’s Phobos variants are distributed by SmokeLoader, a backdoor trojan. This commodity loader typically drops or downloads additional payloads when deployed. In 8Base campaigns, however, it has the ransomware component embedded in its encrypted payloads, which is then decrypted and loaded into the SmokeLoader process’ memory.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/deep-dive-into-phobos-ransomware/
2. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/understanding-the-phobos-affiliate-structure/

#### Publication Date
November 17, 2023

#### Author(s)
Guilherme Venere

enhanced.Incident: Phobos Ransomware Attack by 8Base Group
enhanced.Root cause: The Phobos ransomware is typically deployed through SmokeLoader, a backdoor trojan that decrypts and loads the ransomware payload into its memory. The ransomware contains advanced features such as UAC bypass, persistent configurations, and the ability to disable system recovery and backups. *Phobos is also distributed via hacked Remote Desktop (RDP) connections, a cost efficient dissemination vector for threat groups* (https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.phobos). *Phobos ransomware operates in conjunction with various open source tools such as Cobalt Strike and Bloodhound* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-060a). *Phobos is an evolution of Dharma/Crysis ransomware and may be sold as a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS), managed by a central authority with a single decryption key* (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/understanding-the-phobos-affiliate-structure/). *8Base ransomware operators use a variant of Phobos ransomware with the ransomware component embedded in its encrypted payloads. The ransomware component is then decrypted and loaded into the SmokeLoader process' memory* (https://securityaffairs.com/154383/malware/8base-ransomware-phobos-ransomware.html).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: 8Base group
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Not specified *; however, targeted sectors include municipal and county governments, emergency services, education, public healthcare, and other critical infrastructure entities* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-060a). *The group targets small and medium-size businesses in multiple industries, including finance, manufacturing, business services, and IT* (https://securityaffairs.com/154383/malware/8base-ransomware-phobos-ransomware.html).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Not specified *; Phobos incidents have been regularly reported since May 2019* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-060a). *8Base group has been active since March 2022* (https://securityaffairs.com/154383/malware/8base-ransomware-phobos-ransomware.html).
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001: Application Layer Protocol - Web Protocols
T1059.001: Command and Scripting Interpreter - PowerShell
T1070.004: Indicator Removal on Host - File Deletion
enhanced.Impact: Not explicitly mentioned, however, the ransomware is designed to encrypt files and demand ransom, potentially causing significant disruption and financial losses to the victims. *Phobos ransomware also pivots towards double extortion, launching new leak site to further pressure victims* (https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.phobos). *Incidents have successfully ransomed several million U.S. dollars* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-060a). *Phobos affiliates, including variants like Eking, Eight, Elbie, Devos, and Faust, commonly target high-value servers to increase damage and payout chances* (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/understanding-the-phobos-affiliate-structure/). *Most victims of 8Base group are in the U.S. and Brazil* (https://securityaffairs.com/154383/malware/8base-ransomware-phobos-ransomware.html).
Mitigation: Ensure robust endpoint protection and regularly update signatures to detect and block known threats.
Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) to limit the impact of credential theft.
Regularly back up critical data and ensure backups are stored offline or in a read-only state.
Monitor network traffic for unusual activity that may indicate an infection or attempted intrusion.
Patch all systems regularly to close known vulnerabilities.
Use email filtering solutions to block phishing emails and malicious attachments.
Educate employees on recognizing phishing attacks and safe computing practices.
*Secure RDP ports to prevent abuse* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-060a).
*Implement EDR solutions to disrupt threat actor memory allocation techniques* (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-060a).

Internal checks: Monitor for unusual process creations and injection techniques.
Alert on registry modifications related to persistence techniques.
Detect the presence of known UAC bypass techniques.
External scanning: Monitor for communications with known malicious C2 servers.
Identify and block IPs/domains associated with ransomware campaigns.

title: Agent Tesla Unusual ZPAQ Archive Format Delivers Malware
content:
#### Description
A new variant of Agent Tesla has been discovered that uses the ZPAQ archive and .wav file extension to infect systems and steal information from approximately 40 web browsers and various email clients. ZPAQ is a file compression format that offers a better compression ratio and journaling function compared to widely used formats like ZIP and RAR. However, ZPAQ has limited software support, making it difficult to work with, especially for users without technical expertise. The .NET executable file is bloated with zero bytes, which allows threat actors to bypass traditional security measures and increase the effectiveness of their attack. 

The usage of the ZPAQ compression format raises more questions than answers. The assumptions here are that either threat actors target a specific group of people who have technical knowledge or use less widely known archive tools, or they are testing other techniques to spread malware faster and bypass security software. 

The malware uses Telegram as a C&C due to its widespread legal usage and the fact that its traffic is often allowed through firewalls, making it a useful medium for covert communication. Like any other stealer, Agent Tesla can harm not only private individuals but also organizations. It has gained popularity among cybercriminals for many reasons including ease of use, versatility, and affordability on the Dark Web.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.gdatasoftware.com/blog/2023/11/37822-agent-tesla-zpaq

#### Publication Date
November 20, 2023

#### Author(s)
Anna Lvova

enhanced.Incident: Unusual 'ZPAQ' Archive Format Delivers Malware
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause includes using an uncommon compression format, ZPAQ, to deliver a malicious .NET executable designed to download and decrypt additional payloads. This technique leverages the limited support for ZPAQ to evade traditional detection mechanisms. *The honeypot captured a phishing attempt using a large (1GB) PE file to bypass security controls* (https://isc.sans.edu/diary/rss/30366).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Not specifically identified, but the malware used is a variant of Agent Tesla.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Not specifically mentioned.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: November 1, 2023 – November 20, 2023
MITRE TTPs: T1071: Application Layer Protocol (using Telegram as C&C)
enhanced.Impact: Information stolen from approximately 40 web browsers and various email clients, including credentials and system information.
Mitigation: **Maintain Up-to-Date Security Software**: Ensure that antivirus and anti-malware software are up-to-date to detect and block threats.
**Educate Employees on Phishing**: Conduct regular training sessions to educate employees about phishing attacks and safe email practices.
**Use Email Filtering Solutions**: Implement advanced email filtering solutions to detect and block phishing attempts.
**Monitor Network Traffic**: Regularly monitor network traffic for unusual patterns that may indicate malicious activities.
**Implement Multi-Factor Authentication**: Use multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all critical systems to add an extra layer of security.
**Restrict Command-Line Tool Usage**: Limit the use of command-line tools like ZPAQ to trusted users and environments.
**Regularly Update Software**: Ensure all software, especially security tools, is regularly updated to mitigate vulnerabilities.

Detection Signature.Signature name: Suspicious ZPAQ file in email attachment
Internal checks: Setting1: Scan email attachments for uncommon file formats like ZPAQ.
Setting2: Monitor for files with deceptive extensions like '.pdf.zpaq'.
Setting3: Flag emails with large discrepancies between compressed and uncompressed file sizes.
External scanning: Scan incoming emails for attachments with uncommon formats.
Check for ZPAQ files in email attachments and flag them for further inspection.

title: Ransomware Spotlight Trigona
content:
#### Description
The Trigona ransomware, first tracked by Trend Micro as Water Ungaw, emerged in October 2022 but binaries of the ransomware were seen as early as June of the same year. The group positioned itself as running a lucrative scheme, launching global attacks and advertising revenues up to 20% to 50% for each successful attack.The group was also reported as communicating with network access brokers who provide compromised credentials via the Russian Anonymous Marketplace (RAMP) forum’s internal chats and using the sourced information to obtain initial access to targets.

In April 2023, Trigona started targeting compromised Microsoft SQL (MSSQL) Servers via brute-force attacks. A month later, a Linux version of Trigona was found that shared similarities with its Windows counterpart. The Trigona ransomware is also linked to CryLock due to their similarities in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), ransom note file name, and email addresses used. 

Trigona ransomware targeted government organizations the most, with attack attempts making up 21.4% of total detections, according to feedback from Trend customers who detailed the industries in which they belong. Trigona also targeted enterprises in the technology, retail, fast-moving consumer goods, and banking industries. The group set its sights on small- and medium-sized businesses, which made up more than half of the group’s total victims from April to October 2023. Trigona compromised a total of 33 organizations within the aforementioned period.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/ransomware-spotlight/ransomware-spotlight-trigona

#### Publication Date
November 28, 2023

#### Author(s)
Trend Micro Research

enhanced.Incident: Trigona Ransomware
enhanced.Root cause: Trigona ransomware attacks exploited CVE-2021-40539 vulnerability in Zoho ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus, brute-forced Microsoft SQL (MSSQL) Servers, and used compromised credentials from network access brokers. *They also used tools like Splashtop* (https://www.trendmicro.com/en_vn/research/23/f/an-overview-of-the-trigona-ransomware.html). *AhnLab Security Emergency Response Center (ASEC) identified the use of the CLR extended procedure feature for malicious functions* (https://blackswan-cybersecurity.com/trigona-ransomware-targeting-ms-sql-servers/).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Trigona Ransomware group, potentially affiliated with CryLock and BlackCat ransomware groups.
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Various industries, notably government, technology, retail, FMCG, banking sectors, and SMBs across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and Latin America. *Significant activity detected in the US, India, Israel, Turkey, Brazil, and Italy* (https://www.trendmicro.com/en_vn/research/23/f/an-overview-of-the-trigona-ransomware.html).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: October 2022 – October 2023
MITRE TTPs: T1547.001 - Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys/Startup Folder
T1218.005 - System Binary Proxy Execution: Mshta
T1036.005 - Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location
enhanced.Impact: The ransomware group compromised 33 organizations, targeting government sectors and SMBs, through encrypted data, stolen documents, and contracts published on a leak site. *They used a double extortion scheme, with a leak site on IP address port 8000* (https://www.trendmicro.com/en_vn/research/23/f/an-overview-of-the-trigona-ransomware.html). *The ransomware executed via svcservice.exe and svchost.bat* (https://blackswan-cybersecurity.com/trigona-ransomware-targeting-ms-sql-servers/).
Mitigation: Regularly patch and update all systems and applications to address known vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-40539.
Implement robust password policies and multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Monitor network ports, protocols, and services, and restrict unnecessary exposure.
Employ network segmentation to limit ransomware spread.
Use advanced detection technologies such as AI and machine learning for early detection.
Implement data protection, backup, and recovery measures for quick restoration.
Conduct regular vulnerability assessments and penetration testing.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: **Patch Management**: Ensure all systems and applications are up-to-date with the latest patches.
**Access Control**: Implement MFA and strong password policies. Limit administrative privileges.
**Network Monitoring**: Monitor network traffic for unusual activities, particularly on ports commonly used by the exploited services.
**Network Segmentation**: Isolate critical systems from less secure environments.
**Endpoint Protection**: Deploy endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions to monitor and respond to suspicious activities.
**Backup Strategy**: Regularly back up data and verify the integrity of backups. Ensure backups are not connected to the network.
**Employee Training**: Regularly train employees on phishing and social engineering attack recognition.

Internal checks: Setting1: Monitor failed login attempts on MSSQL (event IDs 18456).
Setting2: Detect unusual spikes in MSSQL login attempts.
Setting3: Ensure MSSQL databases are secured with strong, unique passwords and MFA.
External scanning: Port (1433) open
Unusual login attempts

enhanced.IoCs: Indicators of compromise can be found [here](https://documents.trendmicro.com/images/TEx/articles/trigona-ransomware-iocs78HQqGi.txt). *The group also used the Mimikatz credential dumper and developed a Linux version of their ransomware* (https://www.trendmicro.com/en_vn/research/23/f/an-overview-of-the-trigona-ransomware.html).

title: Operation Blacksmith Lazarus Targets Organizations Worldwide Using Novel Telegram-Based Malware Written in DLang
content:
#### Description
Cisco Talos has discovered a new campaign conducted by the Lazarus Group, called "Operation Blacksmith," which employs at least three new DLang-based malware families, two of which are remote access trojans (RATs), where one of these uses Telegram bots and channels as a medium of command and control (C2) communications.

The RATs are named "NineRAT" and "DLRAT," and the downloader is called "BottomLoader." The campaign consists of continued opportunistic targeting of enterprises globally that publicly host and expose their vulnerable infrastructure to n-day vulnerability exploitation such as CVE-2021-44228 (Log4j). Lazarus has targeted manufacturing, agricultural, and physical security companies. The malware is written in DLang, indicating a definitive shift in TTPs from APT groups falling under the Lazarus umbrella with the increased adoption of malware being authored using non-traditional frameworks such as the Qt framework, including MagicRAT and QuiteRAT.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://blog.talosintelligence.com/lazarus_new_rats_dlang_and_telegram/

#### Publication Date
December 11, 2023

#### Author(s)
Jungsoo An

enhanced.Incident: Operation Blacksmith
enhanced.Root cause: Exploitation of CVE-2021-44228 (Log4j vulnerability) on publicly facing VMWare Horizon servers.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Lazarus Group (North Korean APT group), including the Andariel APT subgroup and Onyx Sleet subgroup *Onyx Sleet subgroup* (https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/lazarus-exploits-log4shell-to-deploy-telegram-based-malware-a-23855).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Worldwide targeting, specifically manufacturing, agricultural, and physical security sectors, including European companies and South Korean physical security firms *European company; South Korean physical security firm* (https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/lazarus-exploits-log4shell-to-deploy-telegram-based-malware-a-23855).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: March 2023 – September 2023 (notable activity periods).
enhanced.Impact: Multiple organizations across manufacturing, agricultural, and physical security sectors were affected, leading to unauthorized access and potential data exfiltration.
Mitigation: Apply patches for CVE-2021-44228 (Log4j) and ensure all systems are up-to-date.
Implement network segmentation to limit exposure of critical systems.
Employ multi-factor authentication (MFA) to secure access.
Use endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions to detect and mitigate malicious activities.
Regularly review and update incident response plans.
Monitor and block suspicious outbound network traffic, particularly to known malicious IPs and domains.
Conduct regular security awareness training to help employees recognize phishing attempts.

Internal checks.Setting2: Monitor application logs for evidence of Log4j exploitation attempts.
Internal checks.Setting3: Validate that all instances of Log4j are configured with mitigations if patches cannot be applied.

Additional Details.Operation Blacksmith involved the deploy: Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini (SecurityAffairs – hacking, APT)

title: UAC-0050 Group Using New Phishing Tactics to Distribute Remcos RAT
content:
#### Description
The UAC-0050 threat group has been found to be using an advanced strategy that allows for a more clandestine data transfer channel, effectively circumventing detection mechanisms employed by Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and antivirus systems.

The group’s weapon of choice is RemcosRAT, a notorious malware for remote surveillance and control, which has been at the forefront of its espionage arsenal. However, in their latest operational twist, the UAC-0050 group has integrated a pipe method for interprocess communication, showcasing their advanced adaptability. The initial attack vector is yet to be pinpointed, though indications lean towards phishing or spam emails. The LNK file is responsible for initiating the download of an HTA file. Within this HTA file lies a VBS script that, upon execution, triggers a PowerShell script. This PowerShell script endeavors to download a malicious payload (word_update.exe) from a server. Upon launching, word_update.exe executes cmd.exe and shares malicious data through a pipe. Consequently, it leads to the launch of explorer.exe with the malicious RemcosRAT residing in the memory of explorer.exe. 

The Remcos version identified is 4.9.2 Pro, and it has successfully gathered information about the victim, including the computer name and username. RemcosRAT removes cookies and login data from the following browsers: Internet Explorer, Firefox, and Chrome.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.uptycs.com/blog/remcos-rat-uac-0500-pipe-method

#### Publication Date
January 4, 2024

#### Author(s)
Uptycs Threat Research

enhanced.Incident: UAC-0050 Remcos RAT: Pipe Method Used for Evasion in Ukraine Attack
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident is the use of a malicious .lnk file to deliver the Remcos RAT malware. This attack is facilitated by leveraging the Windows Interprocess Communication (IPC) pipe method to evade detection by Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and antivirus systems. *CERT-UA#8453 and CERT-UA#8494 alerts detail the techniques used* (https://socprime.com/blog/uac-0050-attack-detection-hackers-are-armed-with-remcos-rat-quasar-rat-and-remote-utilities-to-target-ukraine-once-again/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Ukrainian government agencies
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: December 21, 2023 – January 03, 2024
MITRE TTPs: T1547.001: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
T1553.002: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing
enhanced.Impact: The specific number of records or devices impacted is not mentioned, but the attack has significant implications for Ukrainian government agencies, including potential espionage and data theft.
Mitigation: Use sophisticated email filtering solutions: Automatically identify and eliminate spam messages before they reach users' inboxes.
Educate users: Refrain from clicking on hyperlinks or opening attachments in emails identified as spam.
Deploy network monitoring tools: Identify abnormal communication patterns that could signal the presence of remote access tools.
Regularly review and secure system configurations: Ensure unnecessary services and startup entries are disabled or closely monitored.
Leverage behavioral analysis tools: Identify unusual activities that may suggest attempts by RATs to establish persistence or communicate with command and control servers.
Detailed Steps for mitigation: Email Filtering: Implement advanced spam filters and educate users on recognizing phishing attempts.
Endpoint Protection: Use EDR solutions that can detect and block malicious activities, including unusual pipe usage.
Network Monitoring: Deploy IDS/IPS systems to monitor network traffic for signs of data exfiltration or unusual communication patterns.
System Hardening: Regularly audit and harden system configurations, disable unused services, and remove unnecessary startup entries.
Behavioral Analysis: Implement security solutions that utilize behavioral analysis to detect anomalies indicative of RAT activities.

Internal checks: Setting1: Monitor for the creation of .lnk files pointing to mshta.exe executions.
Setting2: Alert on unusual PowerShell script executions.
Setting3: Monitor for unusual process injections or hollowing activities.
External scanning: Monitor for known malicious URLs and IP addresses associated with the campaign.
Detect and block communications to command and control servers.

enhanced.New Information: *Used CyberChef to decrypt RemcosRAT payload, revealing configuration file* (https://www.uptycs.com/blog/threat-research-report-team/remcos-rat-uac-0500-pipe-method), *UAC-0050 utilized Quasar RAT and Remote Utilities in their attacks* (https://socprime.com/blog/uac-0050-attack-detection-hackers-are-armed-with-remcos-rat-quasar-rat-and-remote-utilities-to-target-ukraine-once-again/), *Meduza Stealer found on dark web* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/remcos-rat-meduza-stealer-cyber-threat-intelligence-roundup/), *UAC-0050 employs new phishing tactics* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/remcos-rat-meduza-stealer-cyber-threat-intelligence-roundup/), *Uptycs detected suspicious LNK file* (https://www.tanium.com/blog/remcos-rat-meduza-stealer-cyber-threat-intelligence-roundup/), *Targeted Ukrainian military personnel* (https://thenetworkcompany.net/uac-0050-group-using-new-phishing-tactics-to-distribute-remcos-rat/), *Used mshta.exe to execute HTML applications* (https://thenetworkcompany.net/uac-0050-group-using-new-phishing-tactics-to-distribute-remcos-rat/), *Remcos RAT version 4.9.2 Pro* (https://thenetworkcompany.net/uac-0050-group-using-new-phishing-tactics-to-distribute-remcos-rat/), *Google Chrome as a target for data harvesting* (https://thenetworkcompany.net/uac-0050-group-using-new-phishing-tactics-to-distribute-remcos-rat/).

title: Cutting Edge Suspected APT Targets Ivanti Connect Secure VPN in New Zero-Day Exploitation  Mandiant
content:
#### Description
On January 10, 2024, Ivanti disclosed two vulnerabilities, CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887, impacting Ivanti Connect Secure VPN (“CS”, formerly Pulse Secure) and Ivanti Policy Secure (“PS”) appliances. Successful exploitation could result in authentication bypass and command injection, leading to further downstream compromise of a victim network. Mandiant has identified zero-day exploitation of these vulnerabilities in the wild beginning as early as December 2023 by a suspected espionage threat actor, currently being tracked as UNC5221. 

Mandiant is sharing details of five malware families associated with the exploitation of CS and PS devices. These families allow the threat actors to circumvent authentication and provide backdoor access to these devices. 

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.mandiant.com/resources/blog/suspected-apt-targets-ivanti-zero-day

#### Publication Date
January 17, 2024

#### Author(s)
Tyler Mclellan  
John Wolfram  
Gabby Roncone  
Matt Lin  
Robert Wallace  
Dimiter Andonov

enhanced.Incident: Ivanti Connect Secure VPN Zero-Day Exploitation
enhanced.Root cause: The root cause behind the incident includes multiple critical vulnerabilities in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances: 1. **CVE-2023-46805**: An authentication bypass vulnerability in Ivanti ICS 9.x, 22.x *affecting multiple versions* (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-46805). 2. **CVE-2024-21887**: A command injection vulnerability. 3. *CVE-2024-21893: A server-side request forgery vulnerability in the SAML component of Ivanti Connect Secure, Policy Secure, and Neurons for ZTA* (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/01/11/etr-zero-day-exploitation-of-ivanti-connect-secure-and-policy-secure-gateways/#:~:text=The%20two%20vulnerabilities%20from%20the,resources%20by%20bypassing%20control%20checks.). 4. *CVE-2024-21888: A privilege escalation vulnerability in the web component of Ivanti Connect Secure and Policy Secure* (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/01/11/etr-zero-day-exploitation-of-ivanti-connect-secure-and-policy-secure-gateways/#:~:text=The%20two%20vulnerabilities%20from%20the,resources%20by%20bypassing%20control%20checks.). 5. *CVE-2024-22024: An XML external entity vulnerability in the SAML component of Ivanti Connect Secure, Policy Secure, and ZTA gateways* (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/01/11/etr-zero-day-exploitation-of-ivanti-connect-secure-and-policy-secure-gateways/#:~:text=The%20two%20vulnerabilities%20from%20the,resources%20by%20bypassing%20control%20checks.). All vulnerabilities were exploited due to the lack of proper security measures, allowing unauthorized access and command execution. *Volexity discovered the attacker modifying legitimate ICS components to evade detection and execute commands* (https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/01/10/active-exploitation-of-two-zero-day-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-connect-secure-vpn/). *Ivanti released an advisory on Jan. 10 detailing active exploitation against fewer than 20 customers* (https://duo.com/decipher/apt-group-targets-ivanti-flaws).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: The attack was carried out by a suspected espionage threat actor group, currently tracked as UNC5221. *Volexity attributes the activity to UTA0178, believed to be a Chinese nation-state-level threat actor* (https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/01/10/active-exploitation-of-two-zero-day-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-connect-secure-vpn/). *Mandiant Consulting CTO Charles Carmakal highlighted the combined exploitation of these CVEs resulting in unauthenticated remote code execution* (https://securitybrief.com.au/story/ivanti-vpn-vulnerabilities-exploited-by-suspected-espionage-group-unc5221). *Mandiant has identified five distinct malicious tools used in these operations, including THINSPOOL, LIGHTWIRE, and WIREFIRE* (https://duo.com/decipher/apt-group-targets-ivanti-flaws).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The victims include organizations using Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances across various industries and locations. *Victims are globally distributed and include multiple Fortune 500 companies* (https://duo.com/decipher/apt-group-targets-ivanti-flaws).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The zero-day exploitation was identified as early as December 2023, with disclosures made on January 10, 2024. *Exploitation was confirmed by Mandiant on January 11, 2024* (https://duo.com/decipher/apt-group-targets-ivanti-flaws).
enhanced.MITRE TTPs: - T1133: External Remote Services - T1190: Exploit Public-Facing Application - T1071: Application Layer Protocol - T1059: Command and Scripting Interpreter
enhanced.Impact: The exact number of impacted records or financial losses is not specified in the blog post. The impact includes unauthorized access and command execution on Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances. *The attacker leveraged exploits to steal configuration data, modify files, download remote files, and reverse tunnel* (https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/01/10/active-exploitation-of-two-zero-day-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-connect-secure-vpn/). *UNC5221 primarily utilized compromised, out-of-support Cyberoam VPN appliances for its command and control, further aiding in evading detection* (https://securitybrief.com.au/story/ivanti-vpn-vulnerabilities-exploited-by-suspected-espionage-group-unc5221). *Over 1,700 devices have been compromised so far* (https://duo.com/decipher/apt-group-targets-ivanti-flaws).

Mitigation.Immediate Actions: - Follow Ivanti's mitigation guidance and apply patches as soon as they are released. - Implement the workarounds provided by Ivanti to secure the affected systems. - Use Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool (ICT) to detect signs of compromise.
Mitigation.Detailed Steps for Mitigation: - Apply the patches provided by Ivanti for CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2024-21893, CVE-2024-21888, and CVE-2024-22024 immediately once available. - Implement network segmentation to isolate vulnerable devices from critical infrastructure. - Regularly update and patch all software and hardware to prevent exploitation of known vulnerabilities. - Monitor network traffic for unusual activities related to the identified vulnerabilities and malware families. - Use YARA rules provided to detect specific malware families associated with this campaign.

Detection Signature.Incident: Ivanti Connect Secure VPN Zero-Day Exploitation

enhanced.Internal checks: - Ensure authentication mechanisms are robust and enforced. - Validate the integrity of deployed web shells and scripts. - Monitor for unauthorized file modifications and abnormal script executions.
enhanced.External scanning: - Scan for open ports commonly used by Ivanti Connect Secure VPN. - Use vulnerability scanning tools to detect exploitation attempts for CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2024-21893, CVE-2024-21888, and CVE-2024-22024.

IoCs.Files: compcheckresult.cgi (LIGHTWIRE web shell); sessionserver.sh (THINSPOOL web shell dropper); lastauthserverused.js (WARPWIRE credential harvester); visits.py (WIREFIRE web shell); sessionserver.pl (THINSPOOL utility script); libsecure.so.1 (ZIPLINE passive backdoor)
IoCs.*Additional Files*: /home/perl/DSLogConfig.pm (Modified Perl module); /home/etc/sql/dsserver/sessionserver.pl (Perl script); /home/etc/sql/dsserver/sessionserver.sh (Script); /home/webserver/htdocs/dana-na/auth/compcheckresult.cgi (Modified CGI file); /home/webserver/htdocs/dana-na/auth/lastauthserverused.js (Modified JavaScript file) (https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/01/10/active-exploitation-of-two-zero-day-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-connect-secure-vpn/)

enhanced.Additional Information: *Ivanti has been collaborating with Mandiant, affected customers, government partners, and Volexity to address these issues. They have identified multiple custom malware families including PySoxy tunneler and BusyBox used for post-exploitation activities* (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/suspected-apt-targets-ivanti-zero-day). *CVSS V3.x Severity Score of 8.2 (High) and CWE-287 (Improper Authentication) are associated with CVE-2023-46805. This CVE is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog* (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-46805). *Volexity detected suspicious lateral movement as early as December 3, 2023, and found outbound connections to IP Geolocation services and Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1* (https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/01/10/active-exploitation-of-two-zero-day-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-connect-secure-vpn/). *UNC5221 planned to maintain its presence on high-priority targets compromised after an eventual patch release, using custom malware families such as ZIPLINE, THINSPOOL, LIGHTWIRE, WIREFIRE, and WARPWIRE* (https://securitybrief.com.au/story/ivanti-vpn-vulnerabilities-exploited-by-suspected-espionage-group-unc5221). *Ivanti plans to release patches from Jan. 22 to Feb. 19, along with a mitigation file* (https://duo.com/decipher/apt-group-targets-ivanti-flaws).

title: ESET Takes Part in Global Operation to Disrupt the Grandoreiro Banking Trojan
content:
#### Description
ESET has worked with the Federal Police of Brazil on an effort to disrupt the Grandoreiro botnet, providing technical analysis, statistical information and known C&C servers to the authorities.

Grandoreiro is a Latin American banking trojan that has been active since at least 2017 and targets Brazil, Mexico, and Spain. Grandoreiro’s operators have abused cloud providers such as Azure and AWS to host their network infrastructure.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/eset-takes-part-global-operation-disrupt-grandoreiro-banking-trojan/

#### Publication Date
January 30, 2024

#### Author(s)
ESET Research

enhanced.Incident: Grandoreiro Banking Trojan Disruption
enhanced.Root cause: The primary vulnerability exploited was the use of cloud providers like Azure and AWS to host C&C servers, facilitating the Grandoreiro banking trojan operations. Additionally, the malware's Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) and the abuse of No-IP’s Dynamic DNS service enabled frequent changes in domain and IP addresses, complicating detection and takedown efforts. Notably, Grandoreiro exhibits rapid development and a modular architecture *rapid development and a modular architecture* (https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/04/28/grandoreiro-how-engorged-can-exe-get/). *It uses advanced evasion techniques* (https://any.run/malware-trends/grandoreiro#:~:text=Grandoreiro%20malware%20technical%20details,-The%20main%20functionality&text=Some%20of%20the%20key%20capabilities,the%20main%20banking%20trojan%20payload.).
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: Grandoreiro Operators (likely a single group or closely cooperating groups)
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: Targets were primarily in Brazil, Mexico, Spain, and Peru *Peru* (https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/04/28/grandoreiro-how-engorged-can-exe-get/). The disruption was led by the Federal Police of Brazil with technical assistance from ESET and cooperation from Interpol, the Spanish National Police, and Caixa Bank *Interpol and the Spanish National Police* (https://www.gov.br/pf/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2024/01/pf-combate-organizacao-criminosa-que-praticava-fraudes-bancarias-eletronicas-contra-vitimas-no-exterior). *Caixa Bank* (https://cert.europa.eu/publications/threat-intelligence/cb24-02/).
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Grandoreiro has been active since at least 2017, with consistent tracking and analysis by ESET since then. The disruption operation was reported on January 30, 2024. *Grandoreiro was first observed in 2016 and tracked by IBM X-Force since March 2024* (https://any.run/malware-trends/grandoreiro#:~:text=Grandoreiro%20malware%20technical%20details,-The%20main%20functionality&text=Some%20of%20the%20key%20capabilities,the%20main%20banking%20trojan%20payload.) *IBM X-Force* (https://cyberinsider.com/grandoreiro-banking-trojan-surges-globally-following-police-disruption/).
MITRE TTPs: T1587.001: Develop Capabilities: Malware – Development of custom downloaders.
T1566: Phishing – Initial access through phishing emails.
T1204.002: User Execution: Malicious File – Victims manually executing phishing attachments.
T1547.001: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder – Persistence mechanism.
T1574.001: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking – Execution through compromised DLL search order.
T1140: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information – Distribution in password-protected ZIP archives.
T1027.001: Obfuscated Files or Information: Binary Padding – Use of enlarged .rsrc sections with BMP images.
T1218.007: System Binary Proxy Execution: Msiexec – Bundling downloaders inside MSI installers.
T1112: Modify Registry – Storing configuration data in the Windows registry.
T1010: Application Window Discovery – Discovering online banking websites based on window names.
T1057: Process Discovery – Discovering security tools based on process names.
T1518.001: Software Discovery: Security Software Discovery – Detecting banking protection products.
T1082: System Information Discovery – Collecting victim's machine information.
T1056.002: Input Capture: GUI Input Capture – Displaying fake pop-ups to capture input.
T1056.001: Input Capture: Keylogging – Capturing keystrokes.
T1114.001: Email Collection: Local Email Collection – Extracting email addresses from Outlook.
T1132.002: Data Encoding: Non-Standard Encoding – Using custom stream cipher for encryption.
T1568.002: Dynamic Resolution: Domain Generation Algorithms – Using DGA for C&C server addresses.
T1573.001: Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography – Symmetrical encryption for communication.
T1571: Non-Standard Port – Use of non-standard ports for distribution.
T1071: Application Layer Protocol – Communication built on top of HTTP(S).
T1041: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel – Exfiltrating data to C&C servers.
T1529: System Shutdown/Reboot – Capability to force a system reboot.
enhanced.Impact: The average number of daily victims was 563, with 551 unique victims, and an average of 114 new unique victims per day. The operation saw multiple arrests and the disruption of the Grandoreiro operation, which had illicitly moved at least 3.6 million euros since 2019 *3.6 million euros* (https://www.gov.br/pf/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2024/01/pf-combate-organizacao-criminosa-que-praticava-fraudes-bancarias-eletronicas-contra-vitimas-no-exterior). Additionally, the trojan stole Google Chrome credentials and abused the fear around COVID-19 through spam *Google Chrome credentials and COVID-19 spam* (https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/04/28/grandoreiro-how-engorged-can-exe-get/). *In March 2024, it launched a massive attack targeting over 1,500 banks' applications worldwide* (https://any.run/malware-trends/grandoreiro#:~:text=Grandoreiro%20malware%20technical%20details,-The%20main%20functionality&text=Some%20of%20the%20key%20capabilities,the%20main%20banking%20trojan%20payload.). *IBM X-Force reported extensive phishing campaigns* (https://cyberinsider.com/grandoreiro-banking-trojan-surges-globally-following-police-disruption/). *The operation caused around 120.000.000 US dollars in losses* (https://cert.europa.eu/publications/threat-intelligence/cb24-02/).
Mitigation: Secure cloud services by implementing strict access controls and monitoring for unusual activities.
Regularly update and patch systems to prevent exploitation by malware.
Use advanced threat detection systems to monitor for unusual traffic patterns indicative of DGA activity.
Educate users on recognizing phishing attempts to prevent initial access.
Implement robust email security to filter malicious attachments.
Use endpoint protection with behavior analysis to detect and block malicious activities such as keylogging and unauthorized screen sharing.
Regularly audit and monitor registry changes to detect unauthorized modifications.

Internal checks: Monitor for DGA-generated domains resolving to cloud IP addresses.
Track registry changes related to malware persistence.
Detect unusual process executions and modifications.
External scanning: Monitor traffic to known DGA-generated domains.
Identify and block IP addresses associated with known C&C servers.

enhanced.Additional Insights: The Grandoreiro trojan uses the RealThinClient SDK for C&C communication *RealThinClient SDK* (https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/04/28/grandoreiro-how-engorged-can-exe-get/). It also employs the EASendMail SDK to manage spam campaigns *EASendMail SDK* (https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/04/28/grandoreiro-how-engorged-can-exe-get/). *Grandoreiro operates as a Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS)* (https://any.run/malware-trends/grandoreiro#:~:text=Grandoreiro%20malware%20technical%20details,-The%20main%20functionality&text=Some%20of%20the%20key%20capabilities,the%20main%20banking%20trojan%20payload.). *It employs a CAPTCHA pop-up to bypass automated scanning and uses DNS over HTTPS to avoid DNS-based blocking* (https://cyberinsider.com/grandoreiro-banking-trojan-surges-globally-following-police-disruption/).
